Definitions used in this course (always correct; never change or restate them differently): turnaround time = completion time − arrival time; waiting time = turnaround time − burst time (= completion − arrival − burst); response time = time of first start on the CPU − arrival time; a LOWER priority number means a HIGHER priority; ties are broken by arrival time, then process number; FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive priority never interrupt a running process, while SRTF, preemptive priority and Round Robin can.

Context from the course material:
[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready process. When a new process arrives with a strictly higher priority than the running one, the running process is preempted and goes back to the ready queue with its remaining time, and the new process runs. An arrival with equal priority does not preempt. Completion times are read off the pieces of the Gantt chart.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. preemptive Priority always runs the arrived process with the highest priority (the lowest priority number). non-preemptive Priority is non-preemptive, whereas preemptive Priority is preemptive. On starvation, non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes, while preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under non-preemptive Priority is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, while under preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption, and preemptive Priority has higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch. Choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap; choose preemptive Priority for systems with urgent processes that must run immediately, such as interactive or real-time work.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § What is the effect of Round Robin on average waiting time? [Round Robin])
The average waiting time under Round Robin is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § How does the size of the time quantum affect Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The quantum decides how Round Robin behaves. If the quantum is very large, longer than every burst, no process is ever preempted and Round Robin becomes FCFS. If the quantum is very small, the CPU spends a large share of its time context switching instead of running processes. The quantum should therefore be large compared with the context-switch time; a common rule of thumb is that about 80 percent of CPU bursts should be shorter than the quantum.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the time quantum in Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The time quantum, or time slice, is the maximum continuous CPU time a process may use before it is preempted and sent to the back of the ready queue. It is typically 10 to 100 milliseconds in real systems. In numericals it is given in time units, for example q = 4.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does the time quantum affect context switches and overhead? [Context switch])
A smaller quantum means more context switches, because processes are preempted more often. If a context switch takes s time units and the quantum is q, the fraction of CPU time lost to switching is about s divided by (q + s). For example, with q = 4 and s = 1, 20 percent of the time is wasted. A larger quantum cuts the overhead but weakens the responsiveness.

[1] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise Round Robin in a few lines. [Round Robin])
Round Robin (RR) serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. It is preemptive: a timer interrupt takes the CPU when the quantum expires. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. Its average waiting time is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn, and its context-switch overhead is the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SJF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. On starvation, it can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Which scheduling algorithm is the fairest? [Comparison])
Round Robin is the fairest in the sense that every process receives equal CPU time slices in turn and none starves. FCFS is fair in order of arrival but not in service quality. SJF and Priority scheduling can treat long or low-priority processes unfairly.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF a priority scheduling algorithm? [Priority])
Yes. SJF is priority scheduling in which the priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst: the shorter the burst, the higher the priority. It therefore also shares the starvation problem of priority scheduling.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How many context switches does a scheduling algorithm cause? [Round Robin])
In a non-preemptive algorithm a switch happens only when a process finishes or blocks, so for n processes there are about n − 1 switches. A preemptive algorithm adds a switch at every preemption. Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. [2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is starvation in CPU scheduling? [Priority])
Starvation, also called indefinite blocking, is when a ready process waits for the CPU indefinitely because the scheduler keeps choosing other processes. It happens in SJF and SRTF when short jobs keep arriving and a long job is always passed over, and in priority scheduling when higher-priority processes keep arriving and a low-priority process never gets its turn. FCFS and Round Robin do not cause starvation because every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. The standard remedy is aging.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does Priority scheduling cause starvation? [Priority])
Yes. A low-priority process can wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving. This is indefinite blocking or starvation. The remedy is aging: gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait for a long time so that they eventually reach the highest priority.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages and disadvantages of SRTF? [SJF])
Advantages: it gives the lowest possible average waiting time among the standard algorithms, and short jobs get a very fast response. Disadvantages: it needs the burst lengths in advance, it causes more context switches than SJF, and long processes can starve. A process that has been preempted must be resumed later, so the scheduler also has to keep track of remaining times.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages and disadvantages of Priority scheduling? [Priority])
Advantages: important processes are served first, and the priority can be tuned to the needs of the system. SJF is itself a special case. Disadvantages: low-priority processes can starve, which is solved by aging; and a preemptive version adds context-switch overhead. Choosing good priorities is also not easy.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the disadvantages of Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The performance depends heavily on the time quantum. Too small a quantum causes many context switches and wastes CPU time; too large a quantum makes it behave like FCFS. The average turnaround time is usually higher than in SJF, and the average waiting time is often higher too. There is more overhead than in the non-preemptive algorithms.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

SRTF and Round Robin differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SRTF always runs the arrived process with the smallest remaining burst time. Round Robin serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. Both are preemptive. On starvation, SRTF can starve long jobs, even more easily than SJF, because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly, while Round Robin cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. Average waiting time under SRTF is the lowest of all the standard algorithms, while under Round Robin it is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn. For context-switch overhead, SRTF has higher than SJF, because every preemption is a context switch, and Round Robin has the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry. Choose SRTF for systems where burst lengths can be estimated accurately and a low average waiting time is the main goal; choose Round Robin for time-sharing and interactive systems where every user needs regular turns.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and SRTF in detail [SJF])
SJF and SRTF differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. SRTF always runs the arrived process with the smallest remaining burst time. SJF is non-preemptive, whereas SRTF is preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while SRTF can starve long jobs, even more easily than SJF, because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under SRTF it is the lowest of all the standard algorithms. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and SRTF has higher than SJF, because every preemption is a context switch. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose SRTF for systems where burst lengths can be estimated accurately and a low average waiting time is the main goal.

SRTF and preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SRTF always runs the arrived process with the smallest remaining burst time. preemptive Priority always runs the arrived process with the highest priority (the lowest priority number). On starvation, SRTF can starve long jobs, even more easily than SJF, because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly, while preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SRTF is the lowest of all the standard algorithms, while under preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SRTF has higher than SJF, because every preemption is a context switch, and preemptive Priority has higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch. Choose SRTF for systems where burst lengths can be estimated accurately and a low average waiting time is the main goal; choose preemptive Priority for systems with urgent processes that must run immediately, such as interactive or real-time work.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. [2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Job First scheduling with an analogy [SJF])
Imagine a photocopy shop where the operator always picks the customer with the fewest pages next. Customers with one page are done almost instantly, so the average time people spend waiting is as low as it can be. That is SJF: among the ready processes, the one with the smallest next CPU burst runs first, with FCFS breaking ties. It is provably optimal for average waiting time. Its weaknesses are that the scheduler must predict burst lengths and that a customer with a hundred pages may keep getting pushed back, which is starvation.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain FCFS scheduling with an analogy [FCFS])
Think of a single billing counter at a canteen. Whoever joins the line first is served first, and the cashier never stops serving one customer to serve another. That is First Come First Served: the ready queue is a FIFO queue, the process at the head gets the CPU, and it keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or requests I/O. It is simple and fair in the sense that nobody jumps the queue, but if the first customer has a huge order, everyone behind them waits. That waiting is the convoy effect, and it is why FCFS usually has a poor average waiting time.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Round Robin scheduling with an analogy [Round Robin])
Think of a single counter serving five customers, where the clerk spends at most two minutes with each person before moving to the next one in line. If your work is not finished, you go to the back of the line and wait for your next turn. Round Robin works the same way: the ready queue is circular, each process gets one time quantum, and when the timer expires the process is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue. Nobody waits forever, so there is no starvation, and short jobs finish quickly, which gives good response time. The price is more context switches.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare the algorithms on starvation [Priority])
FCFS cannot cause starvation, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Round Robin cannot cause starvation either: every ready process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. SJF and SRTF can starve long jobs if short ones keep arriving. Priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving. For the last two, aging is the standard fix.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is starvation in CPU scheduling? [Priority])
Starvation, also called indefinite blocking, is when a ready process waits for the CPU indefinitely because the scheduler keeps choosing other processes. It happens in SJF and SRTF when short jobs keep arriving and a long job is always passed over, and in priority scheduling when higher-priority processes keep arriving and a low-priority process never gets its turn. FCFS and Round Robin do not cause starvation because every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. The standard remedy is aging.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does Priority scheduling cause starvation? [Priority])
Yes. A low-priority process can wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving. This is indefinite blocking or starvation. The remedy is aging: gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait for a long time so that they eventually reach the highest priority.

For short processes both algorithms are kind, but in different ways. SJF picks the shortest job first, so short processes run almost immediately and the average waiting time is the minimum possible. Round Robin gives every process one quantum in turn, so a short process that fits in one quantum also finishes quickly, but it may have to wait for a full quantum of every process ahead of it. SJF wins on average waiting time; Round Robin wins on fairness, response time and freedom from starvation.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and Round Robin in detail [Round Robin])
SJF and Round Robin differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. Round Robin serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. SJF is non-preemptive, whereas Round Robin is preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while Round Robin cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under Round Robin it is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and Round Robin has the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose Round Robin for time-sharing and interactive systems where every user needs regular turns.

Round Robin: preemptive, fair, good response time, no starvation, depends on the quantum, more overhead.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is a context switch? [Context switch])
A context switch is the act of saving the state of the currently running process and loading the saved state of the next process to run. The state, including the program counter, registers and memory-management information, is stored in the process control block (PCB). They are pure overhead: no user work is done during the switch, so systems try to keep them infrequent.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How many context switches does a scheduling algorithm cause? [Round Robin])
In a non-preemptive algorithm a switch happens only when a process finishes or blocks, so for n processes there are about n − 1 switches. A preemptive algorithm adds a switch at every preemption. [2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is a context switch? [Context switch])
A context switch is the act of saving the state of the currently running process and loading the saved state of the next process to run. The state, including the program counter, registers and memory-management information, is stored in the process control block (PCB). Context switches happen whenever the scheduler moves the CPU from one process to another, for example when a Round Robin quantum expires. They are pure overhead: no user work is done during the switch, so systems try to keep them infrequent.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do you calculate waiting time, turnaround time and response time from a Gantt chart? [General])
Read the completion time of each process off the end of its last box on the chart. Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time = turnaround time − burst time. Response time = the start of the process's first box − its arrival time. Then average each column over all processes. An alternative for waiting time is to add up every interval the process spent ready but not running.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Define waiting time, turnaround time and response time [General])
Turnaround time is the total time from when a process arrives to when it completes: turnaround = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time is the total time the process spends sitting in the ready queue: waiting = turnaround time − burst time. Response time is the time from arrival until the process gets the CPU for the first time: response = first start time − arrival time. For non-preemptive algorithms response time equals waiting time, because once a process starts it runs to completion.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says the idle time at the start of a Gantt chart counts as waiting time. Is that right? [General])
No. Waiting time only counts time a process spends in the ready queue after it has arrived. If the CPU is idle because no process has arrived yet, that idle gap belongs to no process. You still draw the idle gap on the Gantt chart, but each process's waiting time is turnaround − burst, where turnaround starts at that process's own arrival time.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. [3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready process. When a new process arrives with a strictly higher priority than the running one, the running process is preempted and goes back to the ready queue with its remaining time, and the new process runs. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. preemptive Priority always runs the arrived process with the highest priority (the lowest priority number). non-preemptive Priority is non-preemptive, whereas preemptive Priority is preemptive. On starvation, non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes, while preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under non-preemptive Priority is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, while under preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption, and preemptive Priority has higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch. Choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap; choose preemptive Priority for systems with urgent processes that must run immediately, such as interactive or real-time work.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In preemptive scheduling the operating system can take the CPU away from a running process before its burst is finished, for example when a timer interrupt fires or when a more urgent process arrives. Round Robin, SRTF and preemptive Priority scheduling are preemptive. Preemption improves response time but adds context-switch overhead and needs care when processes share data.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Which scheduling algorithms are preemptive and which are non-preemptive? [Comparison])
Non-preemptive: FCFS, SJF and Priority (non-preemptive version). Preemptive: SRTF (preemptive SJF), Round Robin and Priority (preemptive version). Multilevel feedback queues are preemptive too.

In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. FCFS is a reasonable choice for batch systems where jobs are not interactive and minimising overhead matters more than response time. It needs no timer and causes the fewest context switches. Round Robin is the better choice when users are waiting at a terminal and need regular turns. If the bursts are all short compared with the quantum, the two behave almost identically.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare FCFS and Round Robin in detail [FCFS])
FCFS and Round Robin differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. FCFS runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. Round Robin serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. FCFS is non-preemptive, whereas Round Robin is preemptive. On starvation, FCFS cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue, while Round Robin cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. Average waiting time under FCFS is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, while under Round Robin it is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn. For context-switch overhead, FCFS has the lowest, because there is no preemption, and Round Robin has the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry. Choose FCFS for simple batch systems where jobs are not interactive and low overhead matters; choose Round Robin for time-sharing and interactive systems where every user needs regular turns.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare FCFS and Round Robin [FCFS])
FCFS is non-preemptive: each process runs to completion in arrival order, so it has very few context switches but suffers from the convoy effect and poor response time. Round Robin is FCFS plus a timer: each process runs for at most one quantum and then goes to the back of the queue. That gives good response time and fairness for interactive users at the cost of more context switches. If the quantum is larger than every burst, Round Robin behaves exactly like FCFS.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is a multilevel queue scheduler? [Comparison])
A multilevel queue scheduler splits the ready queue into several separate queues, such as foreground (interactive) and background (batch) processes. Each queue has its own scheduling algorithm, for example Round Robin for the foreground queue and FCFS for the background queue. There is also scheduling between the queues, either fixed priority or time slicing. A process stays in the queue it was assigned to.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the types of schedulers? [Comparison])
There are three types of schedulers: the long-term (job) scheduler, which admits jobs into memory and controls the degree of multiprogramming; the medium-term scheduler, which swaps processes out of and back into memory; and the short-term (CPU) scheduler, which chooses the next ready process to run and runs very often. FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Why do we need a ready queue and a dispatcher? [General])
The ready queue stores the processes that can run, and the scheduler picks one from it. The dispatcher then actually gives the CPU to the chosen process by switching context, switching to user mode and jumping to the right place in the program. The scheduler decides, the dispatcher acts.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says Round Robin causes starvation. Is this correct? [Round Robin])

Round Robin does not cause starvation: the ready queue is circular, so every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units, where n is the number of processes and q is the quantum. What Round Robin does cause is extra context-switch overhead and a higher average turnaround time than SJF. Starvation is a problem of SJF, SRTF and priority scheduling, where a process can be passed over again and again.

Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. [3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is real-time scheduling, EDF and Rate Monotonic? [Priority])
Real-time scheduling must meet deadlines. Earliest Deadline First (EDF) always runs the ready task with the nearest deadline and is optimal on a single processor when total utilisation is at most 100 percent. Rate Monotonic scheduling gives a fixed priority to each periodic task, higher for a shorter period, and is guaranteed to meet deadlines if the utilisation is below n(2^(1/n) − 1), which is about 69 percent for large n.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Which scheduling algorithm is best for batch systems and which for interactive systems? [Comparison])
Batch systems care about throughput and turnaround time, so FCFS or SJF/SRTF are suitable. Interactive time-sharing systems care about response time, so Round Robin or a multilevel feedback queue is the better choice. Real-time systems use priority-based schemes such as EDF or Rate Monotonic.

The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Highest Response Ratio Next (HRRN)? [SJF])
Highest Response Ratio Next is a non-preemptive algorithm that picks the ready process with the highest response ratio, where response ratio = (waiting time + burst time) / burst time. Short jobs have a high ratio at first, as in SJF, but the ratio of a waiting job keeps rising, so long jobs are eventually chosen. HRRN therefore avoids the starvation of SJF by using aging.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for the response ratio in HRRN? [General])
Response ratio = (waiting time + burst time) / burst time. HRRN runs the ready process with the highest response ratio. The ratio grows as a process waits, so long jobs are not starved.

[3] (wikipedia/Shortest_job_next.txt p.1 [SJF])
Shortest job next. Shortest job next (SJN), also known as shortest job first (SJF) or shortest process next (SPN), is a scheduling policy that selects for execution the waiting process with the smallest execution time. SJN is a non-preemptive algorithm. Shortest remaining time is a preemptive variant of SJN. Shortest job next is advantageous because of its simplicity and because it minimizes the average amount of time each process has to wait until its execution is complete. However, it has the potential for process starvation for processes which will require a long time to complete if short processes are continually added. Highest response ratio next is similar but provides a solution to this problem using a technique called aging. Another disadvantage of using shortest job next is that the total execution time of a job must be known before execution. While it is impossible to predict execution time perfectly, several methods can be used to estimate it, such as a weighted average of previous execution times. Multilevel feedback queue can also be used to approximate SJN without the need for the total execution time oracle. Shortest job next can be effectively used with interactive processes which generally follow a pattern of alternating between waiting for a command and executing it. If the execution burst of a process is regarded as a separate "job", the past behaviour can indicate which process to run next, based on an estimate of its running time. Shortest job next is used in specialized environments where accurate estimates of running time are available.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is very large? [Round Robin])
If the quantum is larger than the longest CPU burst, no process is ever preempted, so Round Robin behaves exactly like FCFS. It then has the convoy effect and poor response time.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is very small? [Round Robin])
If the quantum is very small, the CPU spends most of its time switching between processes instead of doing useful work, so the throughput and the average turnaround time get worse. In the limit it approximates processor sharing, in which each process seems to run on its own slower processor.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the time quantum in Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The time quantum, or time slice, is the maximum continuous CPU time a process may use before it is preempted and sent to the back of the ready queue. It is typically 10 to 100 milliseconds in real systems. In numericals it is given in time units, for example q = 4.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do you calculate waiting time, turnaround time and response time from a Gantt chart? [General])
Read the completion time of each process off the end of its last box on the chart. Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time = turnaround time − burst time. Response time = the start of the process's first box − its arrival time. Then average each column over all processes. An alternative for waiting time is to add up every interval the process spent ready but not running.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Define waiting time, turnaround time and response time [General])
Turnaround time is the total time from when a process arrives to when it completes: turnaround = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time is the total time the process spends sitting in the ready queue: waiting = turnaround time − burst time. Response time is the time from arrival until the process gets the CPU for the first time: response = first start time − arrival time. For non-preemptive algorithms response time equals waiting time, because once a process starts it runs to completion.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says the idle time at the start of a Gantt chart counts as waiting time. Is that right? [General])
No. Waiting time only counts time a process spends in the ready queue after it has arrived. If the CPU is idle because no process has arrived yet, that idle gap belongs to no process. You still draw the idle gap on the Gantt chart, but each process's waiting time is turnaround − burst, where turnaround starts at that process's own arrival time.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Round Robin scheduling with an analogy [Round Robin])
Think of a single counter serving five customers, where the clerk spends at most two minutes with each person before moving to the next one in line. If your work is not finished, you go to the back of the line and wait for your next turn. Round Robin works the same way: the ready queue is circular, each process gets one time quantum, and when the timer expires the process is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue. Nobody waits forever, so there is no starvation, and short jobs finish quickly, which gives good response time. The price is more context switches.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Job First scheduling with an analogy [SJF])
Imagine a photocopy shop where the operator always picks the customer with the fewest pages next. Customers with one page are done almost instantly, so the average time people spend waiting is as low as it can be. That is SJF: among the ready processes, the one with the smallest next CPU burst runs first, with FCFS breaking ties. It is provably optimal for average waiting time. Its weaknesses are that the scheduler must predict burst lengths and that a customer with a hundred pages may keep getting pushed back, which is starvation.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain FCFS scheduling with an analogy [FCFS])
Think of a single billing counter at a canteen. Whoever joins the line first is served first, and the cashier never stops serving one customer to serve another. That is First Come First Served: the ready queue is a FIFO queue, the process at the head gets the CPU, and it keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or requests I/O. It is simple and fair in the sense that nobody jumps the queue, but if the first customer has a huge order, everyone behind them waits. That waiting is the convoy effect, and it is why FCFS usually has a poor average waiting time.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § When is FCFS used? [FCFS])
FCFS is suitable for simple batch systems where the jobs are not interactive, where overhead must be minimal and where the order of arrival is an acceptable order of service. It is also used inside other schedulers, for example for processes of equal priority.

[3] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § First Come First Served (FCFS) [FCFS])
FCFS is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm: the process that requests the CPU first is allocated the CPU first. It is implemented with a FIFO queue. When a process enters the ready queue its PCB is linked onto the tail of the queue; when the CPU is free it is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive: once a process has the CPU it keeps it until it terminates or requests I/O. Processes P1, P2 and P3 arrive at time 0 in that order with burst times 24, 3 and 3. The Gantt chart is P1 from 0 to 24, P2 from 24 to 27, P3 from 27 to 30. If the same processes arrive in the order P2, P3, P1 the waiting times become 6, 0 and 3, and the average drops to 3.00. The average waiting time under FCFS is therefore generally not minimal and varies a lot with the order of arrival. Convoy effect. Under FCFS all the short processes wait for one long process to get off the CPU, like cars stuck behind a slow truck. With one CPU-bound process and many I/O-bound processes, the I/O-bound processes finish their I/O and sit in the ready queue while the I/O devices go idle, then they all run quickly and go back to I/O while the CPU sits idle. The result is lower CPU and device utilisation. FCFS is particularly troublesome for time-sharing systems, where each user should get a share of the CPU at regular intervals.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is throughput? [General])
Throughput is the number of processes completed per unit of time. For example, 5 processes finishing in 20 time units give a throughput of 0.25 processes per time unit. Short jobs raise throughput; a long job lowers it. Throughput is one of the criteria to maximise.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for CPU utilisation and throughput? [General])
CPU utilisation = (time the CPU is busy running processes / total elapsed time) × 100 percent, so idle gaps lower it. Throughput = number of processes completed / total elapsed time. For example, 5 processes finished in 20 time units give a throughput of 0.25 processes per time unit.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages of SJF? [SJF])
SJF gives the minimum average waiting time of any algorithm for a given set of processes, so it is optimal in that sense. It gives very good throughput because short jobs finish quickly. It reduces the convoy effect, since short processes are not stuck behind long ones.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.
