[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between turnaround time and waiting time? [General])
Turnaround time is the total time from arrival to completion, so it includes waiting in the ready queue and actually running on the CPU. Waiting time counts only the time spent in the ready queue. Therefore turnaround time = waiting time + burst time, and turnaround time is always at least as large as waiting time.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Define waiting time, turnaround time and response time [General])
Turnaround time is the total time from when a process arrives to when it completes: turnaround = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time is the total time the process spends sitting in the ready queue: waiting = turnaround time − burst time. Response time is the time from arrival until the process gets the CPU for the first time: response = first start time − arrival time. For non-preemptive algorithms response time equals waiting time, because once a process starts it runs to completion.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between waiting time and response time? [Round Robin])
Waiting time is the total time a process spends in the ready queue over its whole life, including every time it was preempted and had to wait again. Response time is only the time from arrival until the first time the process gets the CPU. In non-preemptive algorithms the two are equal, because the process runs to completion once started. In preemptive algorithms such as Round Robin the waiting time is usually larger than the response time.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])

SRTF is the preemptive version: whenever a new process arrives with a burst shorter than the remaining time of the running process, the running process is preempted. In the textbook example, P1 starts at 0 with burst 8, and at time 1 P2 arrives with burst 4, which is less than P1's remaining 7, so P1 is preempted.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says SJF never causes starvation because every job is eventually the shortest. Is this right? [SJF])
No. If short jobs keep arriving, there is always a job shorter than the long one, so the long job can be passed over indefinitely. Nothing in SJF guarantees that the long job ever becomes the shortest. That is exactly starvation. Aging, which raises a job's priority the longer it waits, is the standard fix.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready process. When a new process arrives with a strictly higher priority than the running one, the running process is preempted and goes back to the ready queue with its remaining time, and the new process runs. An arrival with equal priority does not preempt. Completion times are read off the pieces of the Gantt chart.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. preemptive Priority always runs the arrived process with the highest priority (the lowest priority number). non-preemptive Priority is non-preemptive, whereas preemptive Priority is preemptive. On starvation, non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes, while preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under non-preemptive Priority is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, while under preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption, and preemptive Priority has higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch. Choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap; choose preemptive Priority for systems with urgent processes that must run immediately, such as interactive or real-time work.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain FCFS scheduling with an analogy [FCFS])
Think of a single billing counter at a canteen. Whoever joins the line first is served first, and the cashier never stops serving one customer to serve another. That is First Come First Served: the ready queue is a FIFO queue, the process at the head gets the CPU, and it keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or requests I/O. It is simple and fair in the sense that nobody jumps the queue, but if the first customer has a huge order, everyone behind them waits. That waiting is the convoy effect, and it is why FCFS usually has a poor average waiting time.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Job First scheduling with an analogy [SJF])
Imagine a photocopy shop where the operator always picks the customer with the fewest pages next. Customers with one page are done almost instantly, so the average time people spend waiting is as low as it can be. That is SJF: among the ready processes, the one with the smallest next CPU burst runs first, with FCFS breaking ties. It is provably optimal for average waiting time. Its weaknesses are that the scheduler must predict burst lengths and that a customer with a hundred pages may keep getting pushed back, which is starvation.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Why does Round Robin have higher context-switch overhead? [Round Robin])
Round Robin preempts the running process every time its quantum expires, even if it has only a little work left. Each preemption is a context switch: the CPU state is saved into the PCB, the next process's state is loaded, and caches and the TLB may be disturbed. A process with burst 10 and quantum 1 causes 9 switches by itself, while FCFS or SJF would cause none during that burst. So the smaller the quantum, the more of the CPU's time is lost to switching.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § What is the context-switch overhead of Round Robin? [Round Robin])
Round Robin has the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry context-switch overhead. It is preemptive: a timer interrupt takes the CPU when the quantum expires.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for the context-switch overhead in Round Robin? [Round Robin])
If one context switch takes s time units and the time quantum is q, the fraction of CPU time lost to switching is about s / (q + s). A larger quantum lowers the overhead.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is starvation in CPU scheduling? [Priority])
Starvation, also called indefinite blocking, is when a ready process waits for the CPU indefinitely because the scheduler keeps choosing other processes. It happens in SJF and SRTF when short jobs keep arriving and a long job is always passed over, and in priority scheduling when higher-priority processes keep arriving and a low-priority process never gets its turn. FCFS and Round Robin do not cause starvation because every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. The standard remedy is aging.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare the algorithms on starvation [Priority])
FCFS cannot cause starvation, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Round Robin cannot cause starvation either: every ready process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. SJF and SRTF can starve long jobs if short ones keep arriving. Priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving. For the last two, aging is the standard fix.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does Priority scheduling cause starvation? [Priority])
Yes. A low-priority process can wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving. This is indefinite blocking or starvation. The remedy is aging: gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait for a long time so that they eventually reach the highest priority.

At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is starvation in CPU scheduling? [Priority])
Starvation, also called indefinite blocking, is when a ready process waits for the CPU indefinitely because the scheduler keeps choosing other processes. It happens in SJF and SRTF when short jobs keep arriving and a long job is always passed over, and in priority scheduling when higher-priority processes keep arriving and a low-priority process never gets its turn. FCFS and Round Robin do not cause starvation because every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. The standard remedy is aging.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare the algorithms on starvation [Priority])
FCFS cannot cause starvation, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Round Robin cannot cause starvation either: every ready process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. SJF and SRTF can starve long jobs if short ones keep arriving. Priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving. For the last two, aging is the standard fix.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does Priority scheduling cause starvation? [Priority])
Yes. A low-priority process can wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving. This is indefinite blocking or starvation. The remedy is aging: gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait for a long time so that they eventually reach the highest priority.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Job First scheduling with an analogy [SJF])
Imagine a photocopy shop where the operator always picks the customer with the fewest pages next. Customers with one page are done almost instantly, so the average time people spend waiting is as low as it can be. That is SJF: among the ready processes, the one with the smallest next CPU burst runs first, with FCFS breaking ties. It is provably optimal for average waiting time. Its weaknesses are that the scheduler must predict burst lengths and that a customer with a hundred pages may keep getting pushed back, which is starvation.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain FCFS scheduling with an analogy [FCFS])
Think of a single billing counter at a canteen. Whoever joins the line first is served first, and the cashier never stops serving one customer to serve another. That is First Come First Served: the ready queue is a FIFO queue, the process at the head gets the CPU, and it keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or requests I/O. It is simple and fair in the sense that nobody jumps the queue, but if the first customer has a huge order, everyone behind them waits. That waiting is the convoy effect, and it is why FCFS usually has a poor average waiting time.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Round Robin scheduling with an analogy [Round Robin])
Think of a single counter serving five customers, where the clerk spends at most two minutes with each person before moving to the next one in line. If your work is not finished, you go to the back of the line and wait for your next turn. Round Robin works the same way: the ready queue is circular, each process gets one time quantum, and when the timer expires the process is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue. Nobody waits forever, so there is no starvation, and short jobs finish quickly, which gives good response time. The price is more context switches.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes? [General])
A CPU-bound process spends most of its time computing and has a few long CPU bursts. An I/O-bound process spends most of its time waiting for I/O and has many short CPU bursts. A good scheduler favours the I/O-bound processes slightly, because they need the CPU only briefly and then keep the I/O devices busy, which improves overall utilisation.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between a CPU burst and an I/O burst? [SJF])
A CPU burst is a stretch of time in which a process executes instructions on the CPU. An I/O burst is a stretch in which the process waits for an input or output operation to finish. A process alternates between the two until it terminates. The burst time used in scheduling numericals is the length of the CPU burst. Most real bursts are short, and a few are very long, which is why SJF-style prediction works reasonably well.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between SJF and SRTF? [SJF])
Both choose the process with the least CPU time, but SJF is non-preemptive and SRTF is preemptive. In SJF, once a process starts it finishes its burst even if a shorter process arrives. In SRTF, an arriving process with a shorter remaining time than the running process preempts it. SRTF gives a lower or equal average waiting time but needs more context switches.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says Round Robin with a very large quantum is the same as SJF. Is this correct? [SJF])
No, it becomes FCFS, not SJF. With a quantum larger than every burst, no process is ever preempted, so processes simply run to completion in queue order, which is arrival order. SJF would instead reorder them by burst length.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says in Round Robin the preempted process goes back to the queue before a process that arrives at the same moment. Is this correct? [Round Robin])
No. When a process arrives at the same instant that the running process's quantum expires, the new arrival is added to the ready queue first and the preempted process is placed behind it. Putting them in the wrong order is the most common error in Round Robin numericals, and it changes every waiting time after that point.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise Round Robin in a few lines. [Round Robin])
Round Robin (RR) serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. It is preemptive: a timer interrupt takes the CPU when the quantum expires. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. Its average waiting time is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn, and its context-switch overhead is the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF a priority scheduling algorithm? [Priority])
Yes. SJF is priority scheduling in which the priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst: the shorter the burst, the higher the priority. It therefore also shares the starvation problem of priority scheduling.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare SJF and Priority scheduling [Priority])
SJF is a special case of priority scheduling where the priority is the inverse of the next CPU burst. General priority scheduling lets the priority come from anything, such as importance, memory needs or user type. Both can be preemptive or non-preemptive, both pick the best ready process at every decision point, and both can starve the processes they rank lowest, which aging solves.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Is SJF a special case of priority scheduling? [Priority])
Yes. SJF is priority scheduling where the priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst: the shorter the predicted burst, the higher the priority. That is why SJF shares priority scheduling's main weakness, starvation of the processes with the lowest priority, which in SJF are the long jobs.

First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § When is FCFS used? [FCFS])
FCFS is suitable for simple batch systems where the jobs are not interactive, where overhead must be minimal and where the order of arrival is an acceptable order of service. It is also used inside other schedulers, for example for processes of equal priority.

[3] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § First Come First Served (FCFS) [FCFS])
FCFS is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm: the process that requests the CPU first is allocated the CPU first. It is implemented with a FIFO queue. When a process enters the ready queue its PCB is linked onto the tail of the queue; when the CPU is free it is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive: once a process has the CPU it keeps it until it terminates or requests I/O. Processes P1, P2 and P3 arrive at time 0 in that order with burst times 24, 3 and 3. The Gantt chart is P1 from 0 to 24, P2 from 24 to 27, P3 from 27 to 30. If the same processes arrive in the order P2, P3, P1 the waiting times become 6, 0 and 3, and the average drops to 3.00. The average waiting time under FCFS is therefore generally not minimal and varies a lot with the order of arrival. Convoy effect. Under FCFS all the short processes wait for one long process to get off the CPU, like cars stuck behind a slow truck. With one CPU-bound process and many I/O-bound processes, the I/O-bound processes finish their I/O and sit in the ready queue while the I/O devices go idle, then they all run quickly and go back to I/O while the CPU sits idle. The result is lower CPU and device utilisation. FCFS is particularly troublesome for time-sharing systems, where each user should get a share of the CPU at regular intervals.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

Repeat until the queue is empty.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Why is SJF optimal for average waiting time? [SJF])
SJF is optimal because moving a short job ahead of a long job reduces the short job's waiting time by the long job's burst, but increases the long job's waiting time only by the short job's burst. No. Every process in the ready queue gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units, so no process waits forever. Round Robin is starvation-free; its drawback is overhead from context switches, not starvation.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says Round Robin causes starvation. Is this correct? [Round Robin])
No, that is a common mix-up. Round Robin does not cause starvation: the ready queue is circular, so every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units, where n is the number of processes and q is the quantum. What Round Robin does cause is extra context-switch overhead and a higher average turnaround time than SJF. Starvation is a problem of SJF, SRTF and priority scheduling, where a process can be passed over again and again.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Which scheduling algorithms can cause starvation? [SJF])
SJF, SRTF and Priority scheduling can cause starvation: SJF and SRTF starve long jobs, and Priority scheduling starves low-priority processes. FCFS and Round Robin cannot, since every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. Aging fixes starvation in the first group.

Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

In priority scheduling every process carries a priority number and the CPU always goes to the ready process with the highest priority. In our course a lower number means a higher priority, so a process with priority 1 runs before one with priority 3. Processes with equal priority are served in FCFS order. The main risk is starvation of low-priority processes, which is solved by aging.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Priority scheduling? [Priority])
Priority scheduling assigns each process a priority number and always gives the CPU to the ready process with the highest priority. In this course a lower number means a higher priority, so priority 1 runs before priority 3. Processes with equal priority are served in FCFS order. It can be preemptive or non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Priority Scheduling [Priority])
A priority is associated with each process and the CPU is allocated to the process with the highest priority. Equal-priority processes are scheduled in FCFS order. In this course a lower number means higher priority, so priority 1 runs before priority 3. SJF is a special case of priority scheduling where the priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst. Priority scheduling can be preemptive (a newly arrived higher-priority process takes the CPU immediately) or non-preemptive (the new process is put at the head of the ready queue). Five processes arrive at time 0: P1 burst 10 priority 3, P2 burst 1 priority 1, P3 burst 2 priority 4, P4 burst 1 priority 5, P5 burst 5 priority 2. Starvation and aging. The major problem with priority scheduling is indefinite blocking, or starvation: a low-priority process can be left waiting forever while higher-priority processes keep arriving. The solution is aging: gradually increase the priority of processes that wait in the system for a long time, for example by improving the priority by 1 every 15 minutes, so that eventually even the lowest-priority process reaches the highest priority and runs.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SJF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. On starvation, it can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise non-preemptive Priority in a few lines. [Priority])
Priority scheduling (non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: a higher-priority arrival waits until the running process finishes. On starvation, it can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Its average waiting time is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does FCFS cause starvation? [FCFS])
No. FCFS cannot cause starvation, because the queue is served strictly in arrival order, so every process eventually reaches the head of the queue and gets the CPU. A process may wait a long time behind a long job, but it does not wait forever.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Which scheduling algorithms can cause starvation? [SJF])
SJF, SRTF and Priority scheduling can cause starvation: SJF and SRTF starve long jobs, and Priority scheduling starves low-priority processes. FCFS and Round Robin cannot, since every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. Aging fixes starvation in the first group.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does Priority scheduling cause starvation? [Priority])
Yes. A low-priority process can wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving. This is indefinite blocking or starvation. The remedy is aging: gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait for a long time so that they eventually reach the highest priority.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § What is the effect of Round Robin on average waiting time? [Round Robin])
The average waiting time under Round Robin is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn.

[1] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SJF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. On starvation, it can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SRTF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF, preemptive SJF) always runs the arrived process with the smallest remaining burst time. It is preemptive: a newly arrived process with a shorter remaining time takes the CPU at once. On starvation, it can starve long jobs, even more easily than SJF, because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly. Its average waiting time is the lowest of all the standard algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is higher than SJF, because every preemption is a context switch.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do I order the queue in Round Robin when a process arrives at the same time as a quantum expires? [Round Robin])

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says Round Robin with a very large quantum is the same as SJF. Is this correct? [SJF])
No, it becomes FCFS, not SJF. With a quantum larger than every burst, no process is ever preempted, so processes simply run to completion in queue order, which is arrival order. SJF would instead reorder them by burst length.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between a CPU burst and an I/O burst? [SJF])
A CPU burst is a stretch of time in which a process executes instructions on the CPU. An I/O burst is a stretch in which the process waits for an input or output operation to finish. A process alternates between the two until it terminates. The burst time used in scheduling numericals is the length of the CPU burst. Most real bursts are short, and a few are very long, which is why SJF-style prediction works reasonably well.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes? [General])
A CPU-bound process spends most of its time computing and has a few long CPU bursts. An I/O-bound process spends most of its time waiting for I/O and has many short CPU bursts. A good scheduler favours the I/O-bound processes slightly, because they need the CPU only briefly and then keep the I/O devices busy, which improves overall utilisation.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between SJF and SRTF? [SJF])
Both choose the process with the least CPU time, but SJF is non-preemptive and SRTF is preemptive. In SJF, once a process starts it finishes its burst even if a shorter process arrives. In SRTF, an arriving process with a shorter remaining time than the running process preempts it. SRTF gives a lower or equal average waiting time but needs more context switches.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages of SJF? [SJF])
SJF gives the minimum average waiting time of any algorithm for a given set of processes, so it is optimal in that sense. It gives very good throughput because short jobs finish quickly. It reduces the convoy effect, since short processes are not stuck behind long ones.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the disadvantages of SJF? [SJF])
SJF needs to know the next CPU burst length in advance, which is impossible in general, so it must be predicted. It can starve long processes if short ones keep arriving. The non-preemptive version still lets a long job block a newly arrived short job once the long job has started. It is therefore hard to use as a pure short-term scheduler and is more often used as a model for comparison.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SJF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Job First schedules the ready process with the smallest next CPU burst. When the CPU becomes free, the scheduler looks only at the processes that have already arrived and picks the one with the shortest burst; ties are broken by arrival time. The basic version is non-preemptive. SJF is provably optimal in the sense that it gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare FCFS and Round Robin [FCFS])
FCFS is non-preemptive: each process runs to completion in arrival order, so it has very few context switches but suffers from the convoy effect and poor response time. Round Robin is FCFS plus a timer: each process runs for at most one quantum and then goes to the back of the queue. That gives good response time and fairness for interactive users at the cost of more context switches. If the quantum is larger than every burst, Round Robin behaves exactly like FCFS.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare FCFS and Round Robin in detail [FCFS])
FCFS and Round Robin differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. FCFS runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. Round Robin serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. FCFS is non-preemptive, whereas Round Robin is preemptive. On starvation, FCFS cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue, while Round Robin cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. Average waiting time under FCFS is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, while under Round Robin it is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn. For context-switch overhead, FCFS has the lowest, because there is no preemption, and Round Robin has the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry. Choose FCFS for simple batch systems where jobs are not interactive and low overhead matters; choose Round Robin for time-sharing and interactive systems where every user needs regular turns.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Compare FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin in a table. [Comparison])
FCFS: non-preemptive, simple, no starvation, convoy effect, high average waiting time. SJF: non-preemptive, minimum average waiting time, needs burst prediction, starvation of long jobs. SRTF: preemptive, even lower average waiting time, more context switches, starvation. Priority: preemptive or non-preemptive, serves important work first, starvation of low priority solved by aging. Round Robin: preemptive, fair, good response time, no starvation, depends on the quantum, more overhead.

Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare FCFS and Round Robin [FCFS])
FCFS is non-preemptive: each process runs to completion in arrival order, so it has very few context switches but suffers from the convoy effect and poor response time. Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. [2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

The quantum should be large compared with the context-switch time, so that switching is a small overhead, but small enough to give good response time. [2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise Round Robin in a few lines. [Round Robin])
Round Robin (RR) serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. It is preemptive: a timer interrupt takes the CPU when the quantum expires. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. Its average waiting time is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn, and its context-switch overhead is the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the time quantum in Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The time quantum, or time slice, is the maximum continuous CPU time a process may use before it is preempted and sent to the back of the ready queue. It is typically 10 to 100 milliseconds in real systems. In numericals it is given in time units, for example q = 4.

The performance depends heavily on the time quantum. Too small a quantum causes many context switches and wastes CPU time; too large a quantum makes it behave like FCFS. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages of Round Robin? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is fair: every process gets the CPU in turn. It has no starvation, because every process reaches the head of the queue within a bounded time. It gives good response time, which suits interactive time-sharing systems. It is simple to implement with a circular queue and a timer.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages and disadvantages of Priority scheduling? [Priority])
Advantages: important processes are served first, and the priority can be tuned to the needs of the system. SJF is itself a special case. Disadvantages: low-priority processes can starve, which is solved by aging; and a preemptive version adds context-switch overhead. Choosing good priorities is also not easy.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between a CPU burst and an I/O burst? [SJF])
A CPU burst is a stretch of time in which a process executes instructions on the CPU. An I/O burst is a stretch in which the process waits for an input or output operation to finish. A process alternates between the two until it terminates. The burst time used in scheduling numericals is the length of the CPU burst. Most real bursts are short, and a few are very long, which is why SJF-style prediction works reasonably well.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes? [General])
A CPU-bound process spends most of its time computing and has a few long CPU bursts. An I/O-bound process spends most of its time waiting for I/O and has many short CPU bursts. A good scheduler favours the I/O-bound processes slightly, because they need the CPU only briefly and then keep the I/O devices busy, which improves overall utilisation.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between SJF and SRTF? [SJF])
Both choose the process with the least CPU time, but SJF is non-preemptive and SRTF is preemptive. In SJF, once a process starts it finishes its burst even if a shorter process arrives. In SRTF, an arriving process with a shorter remaining time than the running process preempts it. SRTF gives a lower or equal average waiting time but needs more context switches.

It is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. On starvation, it can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])

On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Round Robin scheduling with an analogy [Round Robin])
Think of a single counter serving five customers, where the clerk spends at most two minutes with each person before moving to the next one in line. If your work is not finished, you go to the back of the line and wait for your next turn. Round Robin works the same way: the ready queue is circular, each process gets one time quantum, and when the timer expires the process is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue. Nobody waits forever, so there is no starvation, and short jobs finish quickly, which gives good response time. The price is more context switches.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Job First scheduling with an analogy [SJF])
Imagine a photocopy shop where the operator always picks the customer with the fewest pages next. Customers with one page are done almost instantly, so the average time people spend waiting is as low as it can be. That is SJF: among the ready processes, the one with the smallest next CPU burst runs first, with FCFS breaking ties. It is provably optimal for average waiting time. Its weaknesses are that the scheduler must predict burst lengths and that a customer with a hundred pages may keep getting pushed back, which is starvation.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain FCFS scheduling with an analogy [FCFS])
Think of a single billing counter at a canteen. Whoever joins the line first is served first, and the cashier never stops serving one customer to serve another. That is First Come First Served: the ready queue is a FIFO queue, the process at the head gets the CPU, and it keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or requests I/O. It is simple and fair in the sense that nobody jumps the queue, but if the first customer has a huge order, everyone behind them waits. That waiting is the convoy effect, and it is why FCFS usually has a poor average waiting time.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is the role of the dispatcher? [General])
The dispatcher is the module that actually gives control of the CPU to the process chosen by the short-term scheduler. Its job has three parts: switching context, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper location in the user program to resume it. Because it runs on every process switch, it should be as fast as possible. The time it takes to stop one process and start another is called the dispatch latency.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Why do we need a ready queue and a dispatcher? [General])
The ready queue stores the processes that can run, and the scheduler picks one from it. The dispatcher then actually gives the CPU to the chosen process by switching context, switching to user mode and jumping to the right place in the program. The scheduler decides, the dispatcher acts.

[3] (wikipedia/Scheduling_computing.txt p.1 [Context switch])
function is the dispatcher, which is the module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler. It receives control in kernel mode as the result of an interrupt or system call. The functions of a dispatcher involve the following: Context switches, in which the dispatcher saves the state (also known as context) of the process or thread that was previously running; the dispatcher then loads the initial or previously saved state of the new process. Switching to user mode. Jumping to the proper location in the user program to restart that program indicated by its new state. The dispatcher should be as fast as possible since it is invoked during every process switch. During the context switches, the processor is virtually idle for a fraction of time; thus, unnecessary context switches should be avoided. The time it takes for the dispatcher to stop one process and start another is known as the dispatch latency.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice.
