[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready process. When a new process arrives with a strictly higher priority than the running one, the running process is preempted and goes back to the ready queue with its remaining time, and the new process runs. An arrival with equal priority does not preempt. Completion times are read off the pieces of the Gantt chart.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between turnaround time and waiting time? [General])
Turnaround time is the total time from arrival to completion, so it includes waiting in the ready queue and actually running on the CPU. Waiting time counts only the time spent in the ready queue. Therefore turnaround time = waiting time + burst time, and turnaround time is always at least as large as waiting time.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Define waiting time, turnaround time and response time [General])
Turnaround time is the total time from when a process arrives to when it completes: turnaround = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time is the total time the process spends sitting in the ready queue: waiting = turnaround time − burst time. Response time is the time from arrival until the process gets the CPU for the first time: response = first start time − arrival time. For non-preemptive algorithms response time equals waiting time, because once a process starts it runs to completion.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between waiting time and response time? [Round Robin])
Waiting time is the total time a process spends in the ready queue over its whole life, including every time it was preempted and had to wait again. Response time is only the time from arrival until the first time the process gets the CPU. In non-preemptive algorithms the two are equal, because the process runs to completion once started. In preemptive algorithms such as Round Robin the waiting time is usually larger than the response time.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is aging and why is it needed? [Priority])
Aging is a technique that gradually raises the priority of a process the longer it waits in the ready queue. For example, the scheduler might improve a waiting process's priority by 1 every 15 minutes. Eventually even the lowest-priority process becomes the highest-priority one and gets the CPU. It is needed because plain priority scheduling, and SJF which is a special case of it, can starve low-priority or long processes forever. Aging guarantees that every process makes progress.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Why is preemptive scheduling needed? [General])
Without preemption, one long or never-ending process could keep the CPU forever and the system would not respond to anyone else. Preemption lets the operating system regain control through the timer interrupt, gives interactive users good response time, and lets urgent processes run immediately. The cost is context-switch overhead and the need to protect shared data from being interrupted midway.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does Priority scheduling cause starvation? [Priority])
Yes. A low-priority process can wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving. This is indefinite blocking or starvation. The remedy is aging: gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait for a long time so that they eventually reach the highest priority.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is multiprocessor scheduling? [General])
Multiprocessor scheduling decides how ready processes are spread across more than one CPU. In symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) every processor runs the scheduler and picks from a shared ready queue, which needs locking to avoid two CPUs grabbing the same process. An alternative is asymmetric multiprocessing, where only one designated processor makes scheduling decisions and the rest execute user code, which is simpler but that one processor can become a bottleneck.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is load balancing on a multiprocessor system? [General])
Load balancing moves processes between the per-CPU ready queues of a multiprocessor system so that no CPU sits idle while another has a backlog. Push migration has a periodic task check the queues and push processes from a busy CPU to an idle one; pull migration has an idle CPU pull a waiting process from a busy one. Load balancing works against processor affinity, since moving a process to balance load also throws away its cache state, so real schedulers trade the two off.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the scheduling criteria to maximise and to minimise? [General])
Maximise CPU utilisation and throughput. Minimise turnaround time, waiting time and response time. In exams, the comparison between algorithms is usually made on average waiting time and average turnaround time. Some systems also care about fairness and about predictability of response time.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do you draw a Gantt chart? [General])
A Gantt chart is a bar showing which process holds the CPU during each interval of time. To draw one, start at time 0 or at the first arrival; at every scheduling point choose the next process using the algorithm's rule; draw its box for the time it runs; write the start and end times under the box edges. If no process is ready, draw an idle box until the next arrival. The completion time of each process is the end of its last box.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says the idle time at the start of a Gantt chart counts as waiting time. Is that right? [General])
No. Waiting time only counts time a process spends in the ready queue after it has arrived. If the CPU is idle because no process has arrived yet, that idle gap belongs to no process. You still draw the idle gap on the Gantt chart, but each process's waiting time is turnaround − burst, where turnaround starts at that process's own arrival time.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do you calculate waiting time, turnaround time and response time from a Gantt chart? [General])
Read the completion time of each process off the end of its last box on the chart. Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time = turnaround time − burst time. Response time = the start of the process's first box − its arrival time. Then average each column over all processes. An alternative for waiting time is to add up every interval the process spent ready but not running.

Both always run the highest-priority ready process. The difference is what happens when a higher-priority process arrives while another is running. In non-preemptive Priority scheduling, a newly arrived higher-priority process waits until the running process finishes its burst. Preemptive gives faster service to important work but causes more context switches; both can starve low-priority processes.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § First Come First Served (FCFS) [FCFS])
FCFS is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm: the process that requests the CPU first is allocated the CPU first. It is implemented with a FIFO queue. When a process enters the ready queue its PCB is linked onto the tail of the queue; when the CPU is free it is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive: once a process has the CPU it keeps it until it terminates or requests I/O. Processes P1, P2 and P3 arrive at time 0 in that order with burst times 24, 3 and 3. The average waiting time under FCFS is therefore generally not minimal and varies a lot with the order of arrival. Convoy effect. Under FCFS all the short processes wait for one long process to get off the CPU, like cars stuck behind a slow truck. With one CPU-bound process and many I/O-bound processes, the I/O-bound processes finish their I/O and sit in the ready queue while the I/O devices go idle, then they all run quickly and go back to I/O while the CPU sits idle. The result is lower CPU and device utilisation. FCFS is particularly troublesome for time-sharing systems, where each user should get a share of the CPU at regular intervals.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § When is FCFS used? [FCFS])
FCFS is suitable for simple batch systems where the jobs are not interactive, where overhead must be minimal and where the order of arrival is an acceptable order of service. It is also used inside other schedulers, for example for processes of equal priority.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Shortest Job First (SJF) and Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF) [SJF])
burst counts. Preemptive SJF is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). When a new process arrives with a next CPU burst shorter than what is left of the currently executing process, SRTF preempts the running process. Non-preemptive SJF lets the running process finish its burst. P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8, P2 at 1 with burst 4, P3 at 2 with burst 9, P4 at 3 with burst 5. P1 starts at 0. At time 1 P2 arrives with burst 4, which is less than P1's remaining 7, so P1 is preempted. Starvation under SJF. A long process can wait indefinitely if short processes keep arriving, because there is always a shorter job to pick; this is starvation (indefinite blocking). SRTF makes it worse because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is lottery scheduling? [General])
Lottery scheduling is a proportional-share algorithm. Each process holds a number of tickets; at every scheduling decision a ticket is drawn at random and the process holding it runs. A process with more tickets is chosen more often, so over time each process receives CPU time roughly in proportion to its tickets. Stride scheduling is the deterministic version of the same idea.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

Lottery scheduling is a proportional-share algorithm. Each process holds a number of tickets; at every scheduling decision a ticket is drawn at random and the process holding it runs. A process with more tickets is chosen more often, so over time each process receives CPU time roughly in proportion to its tickets. Stride scheduling is the deterministic version of the same idea. Priority scheduling (non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Its average waiting time is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, and its context-switch overhead is higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch.

Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready process. When a new process arrives with a strictly higher priority than the running one, the running process is preempted and goes back to the ready queue with its remaining time, and the new process runs. An arrival with equal priority does not preempt. Completion times are read off the pieces of the Gantt chart.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

Round Robin with a suitably small time quantum gives the best and most predictable response time, because every process gets a turn within (n − 1) × q time units. SRTF also gives very good response time to short jobs, but can make long ones wait.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for response time? [General])

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for turnaround time? [General])
Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time. It is also equal to waiting time + burst time. It is the total time from the moment the process arrives until it finishes.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for average waiting time and average turnaround time? [General])
Average waiting time = (sum of the waiting times of all processes) / n, where n is the number of processes. Average turnaround time = (sum of the turnaround times of all processes) / n. Compute each process's own time first, then add them up and divide.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do you calculate waiting time, turnaround time and response time from a Gantt chart? [General])
Read the completion time of each process off the end of its last box on the chart. Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time = turnaround time − burst time. Response time = the start of the process's first box − its arrival time. Then average each column over all processes. An alternative for waiting time is to add up every interval the process spent ready but not running.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Why is a time quantum of 10 to 100 milliseconds used in practice? [Round Robin])
A context switch typically takes on the order of microseconds, so a quantum of 10 to 100 milliseconds keeps switching overhead to a tiny fraction of CPU time while still giving interactive users a turn many times per second. Much smaller and the CPU would spend too much time switching; much larger and Round Robin would behave like FCFS and interactive response would suffer.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the time quantum in Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The time quantum, or time slice, is the maximum continuous CPU time a process may use before it is preempted and sent to the back of the ready queue. It is typically 10 to 100 milliseconds in real systems. In numericals it is given in time units, for example q = 4.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is very large? [Round Robin])
If the quantum is larger than the longest CPU burst, no process is ever preempted, so Round Robin behaves exactly like FCFS. It then has the convoy effect and poor response time.

No. If short jobs keep arriving, there is always a job shorter than the long one, so the long job can be passed over indefinitely. Nothing in SJF guarantees that the long job ever becomes the shortest. That is exactly starvation. Aging, which raises a job's priority the longer it waits, is the standard fix.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says Round Robin causes starvation. Is this correct? [Round Robin])
No, that is a common mix-up. Round Robin does not cause starvation: the ready queue is circular, so every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units, where n is the number of processes and q is the quantum. What Round Robin does cause is extra context-switch overhead and a higher average turnaround time than SJF. Starvation is a problem of SJF, SRTF and priority scheduling, where a process can be passed over again and again.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says SRTF never preempts a process once it has started. Is this right? [SJF])
No, that describes non-preemptive SJF. SRTF is the preemptive version: whenever a new process arrives with a burst shorter than the remaining time of the running process, the running process is preempted. In the textbook example, P1 starts at 0 with burst 8, and at time 1 P2 arrives with burst 4, which is less than P1's remaining 7, so P1 is preempted.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. [2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain FCFS scheduling with an analogy [FCFS])
Think of a single billing counter at a canteen. Whoever joins the line first is served first, and the cashier never stops serving one customer to serve another. That is First Come First Served: the ready queue is a FIFO queue, the process at the head gets the CPU, and it keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or requests I/O. It is simple and fair in the sense that nobody jumps the queue, but if the first customer has a huge order, everyone behind them waits. That waiting is the convoy effect, and it is why FCFS usually has a poor average waiting time.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. Think of a single billing counter at a canteen. Whoever joins the line first is served first, and the cashier never stops serving one customer to serve another. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SJF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. On starvation, it can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is throughput? [General])

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says Round Robin causes starvation. Is this correct? [Round Robin])
No, that is a common mix-up. Round Robin does not cause starvation: the ready queue is circular, so every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units, where n is the number of processes and q is the quantum. What Round Robin does cause is extra context-switch overhead and a higher average turnaround time than SJF. Starvation is a problem of SJF, SRTF and priority scheduling, where a process can be passed over again and again.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does Round Robin cause starvation? [Round Robin])
No. Every process in the ready queue gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units, so no process waits forever. Round Robin is starvation-free; its drawback is overhead from context switches, not starvation.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says in Round Robin the preempted process goes back to the queue before a process that arrives at the same moment. Is this correct? [Round Robin])
No. When a process arrives at the same instant that the running process's quantum expires, the new arrival is added to the ready queue first and the preempted process is placed behind it. Putting them in the wrong order is the most common error in Round Robin numericals, and it changes every waiting time after that point.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says a larger Round Robin quantum always gives better performance. Is this true? [Round Robin])
Not always. A larger quantum reduces context-switch overhead, but once the quantum is larger than every burst, Round Robin becomes FCFS and inherits the convoy effect and poor response time. A very small quantum, on the other hand, wastes time on switching. The best quantum sits in between: large compared with the context-switch time, with about 80 percent of bursts shorter than it.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says Round Robin with a very large quantum is the same as SJF. Is this correct? [SJF])
No, it becomes FCFS, not SJF. With a quantum larger than every burst, no process is ever preempted, so processes simply run to completion in queue order, which is arrival order. SJF would instead reorder them by burst length.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says context switching is free because the CPU is fast. Is this true? [Context switch])
No. During a context switch the CPU saves the old process's state into its PCB and loads the new one's, and caches and the TLB may need to be refilled afterwards. No user work is done during this time, so it is pure overhead. With a very small Round Robin quantum this overhead can take a large share of CPU time.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. [2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready process. At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the time quantum in Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The time quantum, or time slice, is the maximum continuous CPU time a process may use before it is preempted and sent to the back of the ready queue. It is typically 10 to 100 milliseconds in real systems. In numericals it is given in time units, for example q = 4.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is very large? [Round Robin])
If the quantum is larger than the longest CPU burst, no process is ever preempted, so Round Robin behaves exactly like FCFS. It then has the convoy effect and poor response time.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § How does the size of the time quantum affect Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The quantum decides how Round Robin behaves. If the quantum is very large, longer than every burst, no process is ever preempted and Round Robin becomes FCFS. If the quantum is very small, the CPU spends a large share of its time context switching instead of running processes. The quantum should therefore be large compared with the context-switch time; a common rule of thumb is that about 80 percent of CPU bursts should be shorter than the quantum.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages of SJF? [SJF])
SJF gives the minimum average waiting time of any algorithm for a given set of processes, so it is optimal in that sense. It gives very good throughput because short jobs finish quickly. It reduces the convoy effect, since short processes are not stuck behind long ones.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the disadvantages of SJF? [SJF])
SJF needs to know the next CPU burst length in advance, which is impossible in general, so it must be predicted. It can starve long processes if short ones keep arriving. The non-preemptive version still lets a long job block a newly arrived short job once the long job has started. It is therefore hard to use as a pure short-term scheduler and is more often used as a model for comparison.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SJF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Job First schedules the ready process with the smallest next CPU burst. When the CPU becomes free, the scheduler looks only at the processes that have already arrived and picks the one with the shortest burst; ties are broken by arrival time. The basic version is non-preemptive. SJF is provably optimal in the sense that it gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes.

It is preemptive: a timer interrupt takes the CPU when the quantum expires. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready process. When a new process arrives with a strictly higher priority than the running one, the running process is preempted and goes back to the ready queue with its remaining time, and the new process runs. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. preemptive Priority always runs the arrived process with the highest priority (the lowest priority number). non-preemptive Priority is non-preemptive, whereas preemptive Priority is preemptive. On starvation, non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes, while preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap; choose preemptive Priority for systems with urgent processes that must run immediately, such as interactive or real-time work.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What does a real operating system like Linux use? [Comparison])
Linux's default scheduler is the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS), which does not use fixed time quanta. It keeps a red-black tree of ready tasks keyed on "virtual runtime" (CPU time already received, scaled by priority/niceness) and always picks the task with the smallest virtual runtime, which approximates giving every task an equal share of the CPU over time. It is conceptually closer to Round Robin's fairness goal than to SJF or FCFS, but it is not one of the four algorithms used for the numericals in this course.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Which scheduling algorithm is best for time-sharing systems? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is the algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Every user's process gets the CPU for one quantum at regular intervals, so each user sees a responsive system and no one is starved. FCFS is a poor choice because one long job can hold everyone up, and SJF needs burst prediction and can starve long jobs. Real systems often use a multilevel feedback queue, which uses Round Robin within each level.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is real-time scheduling, EDF and Rate Monotonic? [Priority])
Real-time scheduling must meet deadlines. Earliest Deadline First (EDF) always runs the ready task with the nearest deadline and is optimal on a single processor when total utilisation is at most 100 percent. Rate Monotonic scheduling gives a fixed priority to each periodic task, higher for a shorter period, and is guaranteed to meet deadlines if the utilisation is below n(2^(1/n) − 1), which is about 69 percent for large n.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is processor affinity and why does it matter? [General])
Processor affinity means a process is kept on the same CPU across repeated runs instead of being migrated to whichever CPU is free. Each run leaves useful data in that CPU's cache; moving the process to a different CPU invalidates that cache and the data must be reloaded, which costs time. Soft affinity is the scheduler's best effort to keep a process on the same CPU; hard affinity lets a process explicitly pin itself to a set of CPUs and never migrate off them.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is load balancing on a multiprocessor system? [General])
Load balancing moves processes between the per-CPU ready queues of a multiprocessor system so that no CPU sits idle while another has a backlog. Push migration has a periodic task check the queues and push processes from a busy CPU to an idle one; pull migration has an idle CPU pull a waiting process from a busy one. Load balancing works against processor affinity, since moving a process to balance load also throws away its cache state, so real schedulers trade the two off.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says context switching is free because the CPU is fast. Is this true? [Context switch])
No. During a context switch the CPU saves the old process's state into its PCB and loads the new one's, and caches and the TLB may need to be refilled afterwards. No user work is done during this time, so it is pure overhead. With a very small Round Robin quantum this overhead can take a large share of CPU time.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says a larger Round Robin quantum always gives better performance. Is this true? [Round Robin])
Not always. A larger quantum reduces context-switch overhead, but once the quantum is larger than every burst, Round Robin becomes FCFS and inherits the convoy effect and poor response time. A very small quantum, on the other hand, wastes time on switching. The best quantum sits in between: large compared with the context-switch time, with about 80 percent of bursts shorter than it.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says SJF never causes starvation because every job is eventually the shortest. Is this right? [SJF])
No. If short jobs keep arriving, there is always a job shorter than the long one, so the long job can be passed over indefinitely. Nothing in SJF guarantees that the long job ever becomes the shortest. That is exactly starvation. Aging, which raises a job's priority the longer it waits, is the standard fix.

[1] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SRTF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF, preemptive SJF) always runs the arrived process with the smallest remaining burst time. It is preemptive: a newly arrived process with a shorter remaining time takes the CPU at once. On starvation, it can starve long jobs, even more easily than SJF, because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly. Its average waiting time is the lowest of all the standard algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is higher than SJF, because every preemption is a context switch.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SJF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. On starvation, it can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes? [General])
A CPU-bound process spends most of its time computing and has a few long CPU bursts. An I/O-bound process spends most of its time waiting for I/O and has many short CPU bursts. A good scheduler favours the I/O-bound processes slightly, because they need the CPU only briefly and then keep the I/O devices busy, which improves overall utilisation.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between a CPU burst and an I/O burst? [SJF])
A CPU burst is a stretch of time in which a process executes instructions on the CPU. An I/O burst is a stretch in which the process waits for an input or output operation to finish. A process alternates between the two until it terminates. The burst time used in scheduling numericals is the length of the CPU burst. Most real bursts are short, and a few are very long, which is why SJF-style prediction works reasonably well.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between SJF and SRTF? [SJF])
Both choose the process with the least CPU time, but SJF is non-preemptive and SRTF is preemptive. In SJF, once a process starts it finishes its burst even if a shorter process arrives. In SRTF, an arriving process with a shorter remaining time than the running process preempts it. SRTF gives a lower or equal average waiting time but needs more context switches.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare preemptive and non-preemptive priority scheduling [Priority])
Both always run the highest-priority ready process. The difference is what happens when a higher-priority process arrives while another is running. In the non-preemptive version, the newcomer is placed at the head of the ready queue and waits until the current burst finishes. In the preemptive version, the running process is interrupted immediately and the newcomer takes the CPU. The preemptive version responds faster to important work but causes more context switches; both can starve low-priority processes without aging.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive Priority scheduling? [Priority])
In non-preemptive Priority scheduling, a newly arrived higher-priority process waits until the running process finishes its burst. In preemptive Priority scheduling it takes the CPU immediately and the running process is put back in the ready queue. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the types of schedulers? [Comparison])
There are three types of schedulers: the long-term (job) scheduler, which admits jobs into memory and controls the degree of multiprogramming; the medium-term scheduler, which swaps processes out of and back into memory; and the short-term (CPU) scheduler, which chooses the next ready process to run and runs very often. FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is a multilevel queue scheduler? [Comparison])
A multilevel queue scheduler splits the ready queue into several separate queues, such as foreground (interactive) and background (batch) processes. Each queue has its own scheduling algorithm, for example Round Robin for the foreground queue and FCFS for the background queue. There is also scheduling between the queues, either fixed priority or time slicing. A process stays in the queue it was assigned to.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between the long-term, medium-term and short-term scheduler? [Comparison])
The long-term (job) scheduler decides which jobs are admitted into memory, so it controls the degree of multiprogramming. The short-term (CPU) scheduler decides which ready process runs on the CPU next and runs very frequently, so it must be fast. The medium-term scheduler swaps processes out of memory and back in to reduce the degree of multiprogramming. The algorithms FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are all short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.
