[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

Context from the course material:
[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Why does Round Robin have higher average turnaround time than SJF? [Round Robin])
Round Robin interleaves all processes, so a process that could have finished early keeps being paused while others take their turns, which pushes completion times later. SJF lets the shortest job finish completely before starting the next, which minimises the average completion and turnaround time. Round Robin trades turnaround time for response time: every process starts quickly even though most finish later.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Why does Round Robin have higher context-switch overhead? [Round Robin])
Round Robin preempts the running process every time its quantum expires, even if it has only a little work left. Each preemption is a context switch: the CPU state is saved into the PCB, the next process's state is loaded, and caches and the TLB may be disturbed. A process with burst 10 and quantum 1 causes 9 switches by itself, while FCFS or SJF would cause none during that burst. So the smaller the quantum, the more of the CPU's time is lost to switching.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for average waiting time and average turnaround time? [General])
Average waiting time = (sum of the waiting times of all processes) / n, where n is the number of processes. Average turnaround time = (sum of the turnaround times of all processes) / n. Compute each process's own time first, then add them up and divide.

Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. [2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. No, that formula gives the turnaround time. Turnaround = completion − arrival is the total time the process spends in the system. Waiting time removes the time spent actually running: waiting = turnaround − burst. For example, a process that arrives at 0, has burst 3 and completes at 27 has turnaround 27 but waiting time 24.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says FCFS is always the worst algorithm for average waiting time. Is that right? [FCFS])
Not always. FCFS is generally poor, but its result depends on arrival order. If the processes happen to arrive shortest first, FCFS produces exactly the SJF order and the optimal average waiting time.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages of FCFS? [FCFS])
FCFS is very simple to understand and implement with a FIFO queue. It is fair in the sense that processes are served strictly in the order they arrive. It has no starvation, because every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. It has the lowest scheduling and context-switch overhead, because there is no preemption.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the disadvantages of FCFS? [FCFS])
The average waiting time under FCFS is often long and depends heavily on the arrival order. A long process at the front makes every short process behind it wait, which is the convoy effect. FCFS is non-preemptive, so it gives poor response time and is unsuitable for interactive time-sharing systems. It also lowers CPU and I/O device utilisation when CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes are mixed.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is very small? [Round Robin])
If the quantum is very small, the CPU spends most of its time switching between processes instead of doing useful work, so the throughput and the average turnaround time get worse. In the limit it approximates processor sharing, in which each process seems to run on its own slower processor.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is very large? [Round Robin])
If the quantum is larger than the longest CPU burst, no process is ever preempted, so Round Robin behaves exactly like FCFS. It then has the convoy effect and poor response time.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the time quantum in Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The time quantum, or time slice, is the maximum continuous CPU time a process may use before it is preempted and sent to the back of the ready queue. It is typically 10 to 100 milliseconds in real systems. In numericals it is given in time units, for example q = 4.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. preemptive Priority always runs the arrived process with the highest priority (the lowest priority number). non-preemptive Priority is non-preemptive, whereas preemptive Priority is preemptive. On starvation, non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes, while preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under non-preemptive Priority is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, while under preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption, and preemptive Priority has higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch. Choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap; choose preemptive Priority for systems with urgent processes that must run immediately, such as interactive or real-time work.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says in Round Robin the preempted process goes back to the queue before a process that arrives at the same moment. Is this correct? [Round Robin])
No. When a process arrives at the same instant that the running process's quantum expires, the new arrival is added to the ready queue first and the preempted process is placed behind it. Putting them in the wrong order is the most common error in Round Robin numericals, and it changes every waiting time after that point.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do I order the queue in Round Robin when a process arrives at the same time as a quantum expires? [Round Robin])
The newly arrived process goes into the ready queue before the preempted process is placed at the back. So if P3 arrives at exactly the moment P1's quantum ends, the queue becomes P3 followed by P1. This rule is a common source of mistakes in Round Robin numericals.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says Round Robin with a very large quantum is the same as SJF. Is this correct? [SJF])
No, it becomes FCFS, not SJF. With a quantum larger than every burst, no process is ever preempted, so processes simply run to completion in queue order, which is arrival order. SJF would instead reorder them by burst length.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for the exponential average used to predict the next CPU burst? [General])
τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n), where t(n) is the length of the most recent actual CPU burst, τ(n) is the previous prediction, and α is a weight between 0 and 1, commonly 1/2. With α = 0 the prediction never changes; with α = 1 only the last burst counts.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § How is the length of the next CPU burst predicted in SJF? [SJF])
Since the scheduler cannot know the future, it predicts the next burst as an exponential average of the past ones: τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n). Here t(n) is the actual length of the most recent burst, τ(n) is the previous prediction, and α is between 0 and 1, commonly 1/2. With α = 0 the prediction never changes; with α = 1 only the last burst matters. With α = 1/2, recent and past history count equally.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Does SJF need to know the burst time in advance? [SJF])
SJF needs the next CPU burst length in advance, which in practice must be predicted, for example with an exponential average of past bursts.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Which scheduling algorithm is the fairest? [Comparison])
Round Robin is the fairest in the sense that every process receives equal CPU time slices in turn and none starves. FCFS is fair in order of arrival but not in service quality. SJF and Priority scheduling can treat long or low-priority processes unfairly.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF a priority scheduling algorithm? [Priority])
Yes. SJF is priority scheduling in which the priority is the inverse of the predicted next CPU burst: the shorter the burst, the higher the priority. It therefore also shares the starvation problem of priority scheduling.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How many context switches does a scheduling algorithm cause? [Round Robin])
In a non-preemptive algorithm a switch happens only when a process finishes or blocks, so for n processes there are about n − 1 switches. A preemptive algorithm adds a switch at every preemption. In Round Robin a process with burst b and quantum q is interrupted about ⌈b/q⌉ − 1 times. The more preemptions, the larger the overhead.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Why do we need a ready queue and a dispatcher? [General])
The ready queue stores the processes that can run, and the scheduler picks one from it. The dispatcher then actually gives the CPU to the chosen process by switching context, switching to user mode and jumping to the right place in the program. The scheduler decides, the dispatcher acts.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the ready queue? [Comparison])
The ready queue holds all processes that are in memory, ready to run and waiting only for the CPU. It is usually a linked list of process control blocks. How it is ordered depends on the algorithm: arrival order for FCFS, burst length for SJF, priority for Priority scheduling and a circular FIFO order for Round Robin.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is the role of the dispatcher? [General])
The dispatcher is the module that actually gives control of the CPU to the process chosen by the short-term scheduler. Its job has three parts: switching context, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper location in the user program to resume it. Because it runs on every process switch, it should be as fast as possible. The time it takes to stop one process and start another is called the dispatch latency.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. [3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. [3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Why does Round Robin have higher average turnaround time than SJF? [Round Robin])
Round Robin interleaves all processes, so a process that could have finished early keeps being paused while others take their turns, which pushes completion times later. SJF lets the shortest job finish completely before starting the next, which minimises the average completion and turnaround time. Round Robin trades turnaround time for response time: every process starts quickly even though most finish later.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Why does Round Robin have higher context-switch overhead? [Round Robin])
Round Robin preempts the running process every time its quantum expires, even if it has only a little work left. Each preemption is a context switch: the CPU state is saved into the PCB, the next process's state is loaded, and caches and the TLB may be disturbed. A process with burst 10 and quantum 1 causes 9 switches by itself, while FCFS or SJF would cause none during that burst. So the smaller the quantum, the more of the CPU's time is lost to switching.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for average waiting time and average turnaround time? [General])
Average waiting time = (sum of the waiting times of all processes) / n, where n is the number of processes. Average turnaround time = (sum of the turnaround times of all processes) / n. Compute each process's own time first, then add them up and divide.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. [2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says context switching is free because the CPU is fast. Is this true? [Context switch])
No. During a context switch the CPU saves the old process's state into its PCB and loads the new one's, and caches and the TLB may need to be refilled afterwards. No user work is done during this time, so it is pure overhead. With a very small Round Robin quantum this overhead can take a large share of CPU time.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says a larger Round Robin quantum always gives better performance. Is this true? [Round Robin])
Not always. A larger quantum reduces context-switch overhead, but once the quantum is larger than every burst, Round Robin becomes FCFS and inherits the convoy effect and poor response time. A very small quantum, on the other hand, wastes time on switching. The best quantum sits in between: large compared with the context-switch time, with about 80 percent of bursts shorter than it.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says SJF never causes starvation because every job is eventually the shortest. Is this right? [SJF])
No. If short jobs keep arriving, there is always a job shorter than the long one, so the long job can be passed over indefinitely. Nothing in SJF guarantees that the long job ever becomes the shortest. That is exactly starvation. Aging, which raises a job's priority the longer it waits, is the standard fix.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is aging and why is it needed? [Priority])
Aging is a technique that gradually raises the priority of a process the longer it waits in the ready queue. For example, the scheduler might improve a waiting process's priority by 1 every 15 minutes. Eventually even the lowest-priority process becomes the highest-priority one and gets the CPU. It is needed because plain priority scheduling, and SJF which is a special case of it, can starve low-priority or long processes forever. Aging guarantees that every process makes progress.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Why is preemptive scheduling needed? [General])
Without preemption, one long or never-ending process could keep the CPU forever and the system would not respond to anyone else. Preemption lets the operating system regain control through the timer interrupt, gives interactive users good response time, and lets urgent processes run immediately. The cost is context-switch overhead and the need to protect shared data from being interrupted midway.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the scheduling criteria to maximise and to minimise? [General])
Maximise CPU utilisation and throughput. Minimise turnaround time, waiting time and response time. In exams, the comparison between algorithms is usually made on average waiting time and average turnaround time. Some systems also care about fairness and about predictability of response time.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Give pseudocode for Round Robin scheduling. [Round Robin])
Pseudocode: put all arrived processes in a FIFO queue; while the queue is not empty: remove the process at the head; run it for min(quantum, remaining time); advance the clock by that amount; enqueue any processes that arrived during this time; if the process still has remaining time, enqueue it at the tail, otherwise record completion time = clock; if the queue is empty but processes are still to arrive, advance the clock to the next arrival.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise Round Robin in a few lines. [Round Robin])
Round Robin (RR) serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. It is preemptive: a timer interrupt takes the CPU when the quantum expires. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. Its average waiting time is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn, and its context-switch overhead is the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is multiprocessor scheduling? [General])
Multiprocessor scheduling decides how ready processes are spread across more than one CPU. In symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) every processor runs the scheduler and picks from a shared ready queue, which needs locking to avoid two CPUs grabbing the same process. An alternative is asymmetric multiprocessing, where only one designated processor makes scheduling decisions and the rest execute user code, which is simpler but that one processor can become a bottleneck.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is load balancing on a multiprocessor system? [General])
Load balancing moves processes between the per-CPU ready queues of a multiprocessor system so that no CPU sits idle while another has a backlog. Push migration has a periodic task check the queues and push processes from a busy CPU to an idle one; pull migration has an idle CPU pull a waiting process from a busy one. Load balancing works against processor affinity, since moving a process to balance load also throws away its cache state, so real schedulers trade the two off.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. On starvation, it can starve long jobs, even more easily than SJF, because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly. Its average waiting time is the lowest of all the standard algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is higher than SJF, because every preemption is a context switch.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Why is SJF optimal? [SJF])
Moving a short job ahead of a long job decreases the short job's waiting time by the long job's burst and increases the long job's waiting time by only the short job's burst. Since the short burst is smaller, the total waiting time decreases with every such swap. When no more swaps are possible the jobs are in order of increasing burst, which gives the minimum total and therefore the minimum average waiting time.

When a new process arrives with a strictly higher priority than the running one, the running process is preempted and goes back to the ready queue with its remaining time, and the new process runs. An arrival with equal priority does not preempt. Completion times are read off the pieces of the Gantt chart.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. preemptive Priority always runs the arrived process with the highest priority (the lowest priority number). non-preemptive Priority is non-preemptive, whereas preemptive Priority is preemptive. On starvation, non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes, while preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under non-preemptive Priority is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, while under preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption, and preemptive Priority has higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch. Choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap; choose preemptive Priority for systems with urgent processes that must run immediately, such as interactive or real-time work.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. [2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is CPU utilisation and how is it calculated? [General])
CPU utilisation is the percentage of time the CPU is busy running processes. In a Gantt chart it is the total time the CPU spends running processes divided by the total length of the chart, multiplied by 100. Idle gaps, when no process has arrived yet, reduce it. For example, if the CPU runs for 16 of 20 time units, the utilisation is 80 percent.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for CPU utilisation and throughput? [General])
CPU utilisation = (time the CPU is busy running processes / total elapsed time) × 100 percent, so idle gaps lower it. Throughput = number of processes completed / total elapsed time. For example, 5 processes finished in 20 time units give a throughput of 0.25 processes per time unit.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

The quantum decides how Round Robin behaves. If the quantum is very large, longer than every burst, no process is ever preempted and Round Robin becomes FCFS. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the ready queue? [Comparison])
The ready queue holds all processes that are in memory, ready to run and waiting only for the CPU. It is usually a linked list of process control blocks. How it is ordered depends on the algorithm: arrival order for FCFS, burst length for SJF, priority for Priority scheduling and a circular FIFO order for Round Robin.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Why do we need a ready queue and a dispatcher? [General])
The ready queue stores the processes that can run, and the scheduler picks one from it. The dispatcher then actually gives the CPU to the chosen process by switching context, switching to user mode and jumping to the right place in the program. The scheduler decides, the dispatcher acts.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is a multilevel queue scheduler? [Comparison])
A multilevel queue scheduler splits the ready queue into several separate queues, such as foreground (interactive) and background (batch) processes. Each queue has its own scheduling algorithm, for example Round Robin for the foreground queue and FCFS for the background queue. There is also scheduling between the queues, either fixed priority or time slicing. A process stays in the queue it was assigned to.

[1] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SJF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. On starvation, it can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SRTF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF, preemptive SJF) always runs the arrived process with the smallest remaining burst time. It is preemptive: a newly arrived process with a shorter remaining time takes the CPU at once. On starvation, it can starve long jobs, even more easily than SJF, because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly. Its average waiting time is the lowest of all the standard algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is higher than SJF, because every preemption is a context switch.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

Scheduling decisions can happen at four moments: when a process switches from running to waiting, for example on an I/O request; from running to ready, for example on a timer interrupt; from waiting to ready, when its I/O completes; and when a process terminates. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for CPU utilisation and throughput? [General])
CPU utilisation = (time the CPU is busy running processes / total elapsed time) × 100 percent, so idle gaps lower it. Throughput = number of processes completed / total elapsed time. For example, 5 processes finished in 20 time units give a throughput of 0.25 processes per time unit.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is CPU utilisation and how is it calculated? [General])
CPU utilisation is the percentage of time the CPU is busy running processes. In a Gantt chart it is the total time the CPU spends running processes divided by the total length of the chart, multiplied by 100. Idle gaps, when no process has arrived yet, reduce it. For example, if the CPU runs for 16 of 20 time units, the utilisation is 80 percent.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is throughput? [General])
Throughput is the number of processes completed per unit of time. For example, 5 processes finishing in 20 time units give a throughput of 0.25 processes per time unit. Short jobs raise throughput; a long job lowers it. Throughput is one of the criteria to maximise.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § What is the effect of Round Robin on average waiting time? [Round Robin])

Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.
