The ready queue stores the processes that can run, and the scheduler picks one from it. The dispatcher then actually gives the CPU to the chosen process by switching context, switching to user mode and jumping to the right place in the program. The scheduler decides, the dispatcher acts.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the ready queue? [Comparison])
The ready queue holds all processes that are in memory, ready to run and waiting only for the CPU. It is usually a linked list of process control blocks. How it is ordered depends on the algorithm: arrival order for FCFS, burst length for SJF, priority for Priority scheduling and a circular FIFO order for Round Robin.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is the role of the dispatcher? [General])
The dispatcher is the module that actually gives control of the CPU to the process chosen by the short-term scheduler. Its job has three parts: switching context, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper location in the user program to resume it. Because it runs on every process switch, it should be as fast as possible. The time it takes to stop one process and start another is called the dispatch latency.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

Processor affinity means a process is kept on the same CPU across repeated runs instead of being migrated to whichever CPU is free. Each run leaves useful data in that CPU's cache; moving the process to a different CPU invalidates that cache and the data must be reloaded, which costs time. Soft affinity is the scheduler's best effort to keep a process on the same CPU; hard affinity lets a process explicitly pin itself to a set of CPUs and never migrate off them.

Load balancing moves processes between the per-CPU ready queues of a multiprocessor system so that no CPU sits idle while another has a backlog. Load balancing works against processor affinity, since moving a process to balance load also throws away its cache state, so real schedulers trade the two off.

SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

The dispatcher is the module that actually gives control of the CPU to the process chosen by the short-term scheduler. Its job has three parts: switching context, switching to user mode, and jumping to the proper location in the user program to resume it. function is the dispatcher, which is the module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler. The functions of a dispatcher involve the following: Context switches, in which the dispatcher saves the state (also known as context) of the process or thread that was previously running; the dispatcher then loads the initial or previously saved state of the new process. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is a multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ)? [MLFQ])
A multilevel feedback queue is like a multilevel queue except that processes can move between queues based on their behaviour. A new process enters the top queue. A process that uses its full time allotment at a level moves down, so CPU-bound jobs sink to lower-priority queues. Interactive jobs that give up the CPU early stay high. Periodically all jobs may be boosted to the top queue to prevent starvation.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is a multilevel feedback queue? [Priority])
A multilevel feedback queue has several ready queues with different priorities, and it lets processes move between them. A process that uses its whole quantum, behaving like a CPU-bound job, is moved down to a lower-priority queue. A process that waits too long in a lower queue is moved up, which is a form of aging. Interactive, I/O-bound processes therefore stay in the high-priority queues and get good response time, and no process starves.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the rules of MLFQ? [Priority])
The standard rules are: if the priority of A is higher than B, A runs; if the priorities are equal, they run in Round Robin using the quantum of their queue; a new job enters the highest-priority queue; once a job uses up its time allotment at a level it moves down one queue; and after some period S all jobs are moved to the topmost queue (the priority boost), which prevents starvation and handles jobs whose behaviour changes.

Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. External priorities come from outside the operating system, such as the importance of the process, the type or amount of funds being paid for computer use, or the department sponsoring the work. Priorities can be static (fixed) or dynamic (change over time).

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § What is the effect of Round Robin on average waiting time? [Round Robin])
The average waiting time under Round Robin is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for turnaround time? [General])
Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time. It is also equal to waiting time + burst time. It is the total time from the moment the process arrives until it finishes.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for average waiting time and average turnaround time? [General])
Average waiting time = (sum of the waiting times of all processes) / n, where n is the number of processes. Average turnaround time = (sum of the turnaround times of all processes) / n. Compute each process's own time first, then add them up and divide.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do you calculate waiting time, turnaround time and response time from a Gantt chart? [General])
Read the completion time of each process off the end of its last box on the chart. Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time = turnaround time − burst time. Response time = the start of the process's first box − its arrival time. Then average each column over all processes. An alternative for waiting time is to add up every interval the process spent ready but not running.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is very large? [Round Robin])
If the quantum is larger than the longest CPU burst, no process is ever preempted, so Round Robin behaves exactly like FCFS. It then has the convoy effect and poor response time.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is very small? [Round Robin])
If the quantum is very small, the CPU spends most of its time switching between processes instead of doing useful work, so the throughput and the average turnaround time get worse. In the limit it approximates processor sharing, in which each process seems to run on its own slower processor.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the time quantum in Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The time quantum, or time slice, is the maximum continuous CPU time a process may use before it is preempted and sent to the back of the ready queue. It is typically 10 to 100 milliseconds in real systems. In numericals it is given in time units, for example q = 4.

[1] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SJF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. On starvation, it can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SRTF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF, preemptive SJF) always runs the arrived process with the smallest remaining burst time. It is preemptive: a newly arrived process with a shorter remaining time takes the CPU at once. On starvation, it can starve long jobs, even more easily than SJF, because a long job can also be preempted repeatedly. Its average waiting time is the lowest of all the standard algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is higher than SJF, because every preemption is a context switch.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Why is preemptive scheduling needed? [General])
Without preemption, one long or never-ending process could keep the CPU forever and the system would not respond to anyone else. Preemption lets the operating system regain control through the timer interrupt, gives interactive users good response time, and lets urgent processes run immediately. The cost is context-switch overhead and the need to protect shared data from being interrupted midway.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In preemptive scheduling the operating system can take the CPU away from a running process before its burst is finished, for example when a timer interrupt fires or when a more urgent process arrives. Round Robin, SRTF and preemptive Priority scheduling are preemptive. Preemption improves response time but adds context-switch overhead and needs care when processes share data.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is aging and why is it needed? [Priority])
Aging is a technique that gradually raises the priority of a process the longer it waits in the ready queue. For example, the scheduler might improve a waiting process's priority by 1 every 15 minutes. Eventually even the lowest-priority process becomes the highest-priority one and gets the CPU. It is needed because plain priority scheduling, and SJF which is a special case of it, can starve low-priority or long processes forever. Aging guarantees that every process makes progress.

Advantages: important processes are served first, and the priority can be tuned to the needs of the system. SJF is itself a special case. Disadvantages: it needs the burst lengths in advance, it causes more context switches than SJF, and long processes can starve. A process that has been preempted must be resumed later, so the scheduler also has to keep track of remaining times.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the disadvantages of Round Robin? [Round Robin])
The performance depends heavily on the time quantum. Too small a quantum causes many context switches and wastes CPU time; too large a quantum makes it behave like FCFS. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is CPU scheduling? [General])
CPU scheduling is the operating system's decision about which process in the ready queue gets the CPU next. Because a process alternates between CPU bursts and I/O bursts, the CPU would sit idle during I/O if nothing else could run. The scheduler keeps the CPU busy by switching to another ready process whenever the running one blocks, finishes, or is preempted. The goal is to maximise CPU utilisation and throughput while minimising waiting time, turnaround time and response time.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

In preemptive scheduling the operating system can take the CPU away from a running process before its burst is finished, for example when a timer interrupt fires or when a more urgent process arrives. Round Robin, SRTF and preemptive Priority scheduling are preemptive. Preemption improves response time but adds context-switch overhead and needs care when processes share data.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling? [SJF])
In non-preemptive (cooperative) scheduling, once a process gets the CPU it keeps it until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. In preemptive scheduling the operating system can take the CPU away from a running process, for example when a timer interrupt fires or when a more important process arrives. FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive. Round Robin and SRTF are preemptive, and priority scheduling can be either. Preemption improves response time but adds context-switch overhead.

FCFS: non-preemptive, simple, no starvation, convoy effect, high average waiting time. SJF: non-preemptive, minimum average waiting time, needs burst prediction, starvation of long jobs. [2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare FCFS and SJF [FCFS])
FCFS serves processes in arrival order and SJF serves the shortest burst first. SJF is optimal for average waiting time, but it needs burst lengths to be known or predicted and it can starve long jobs. FCFS needs no prediction and never starves anyone, but it suffers from the convoy effect.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare FCFS and Round Robin [FCFS])
FCFS is non-preemptive: each process runs to completion in arrival order, so it has very few context switches but suffers from the convoy effect and poor response time. Round Robin is FCFS plus a timer: each process runs for at most one quantum and then goes to the back of the queue. That gives good response time and fairness for interactive users at the cost of more context switches. If the quantum is larger than every burst, Round Robin behaves exactly like FCFS.

First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. [2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare FCFS and SJF [FCFS])
FCFS serves processes in arrival order and SJF serves the shortest burst first. SJF is optimal for average waiting time, but it needs burst lengths to be known or predicted and it can starve long jobs. FCFS needs no prediction and never starves anyone, but it suffers from the convoy effect.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SJF in a few lines. [SJF])
Shortest Job First (SJF, non-preemptive) picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. It is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it finishes its burst even if a shorter job arrives. On starvation, it can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving. Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How are threads scheduled? [Round Robin])
Kernel-level threads are scheduled directly by the OS scheduler like any other schedulable unit. User-level threads are invisible to the OS and are scheduled onto kernel threads by a thread library using its own scheme, such as a simple Round Robin among the user threads of a process; the kernel only ever sees and schedules the underlying kernel thread(s). This two-level scheduling is why some thread libraries are described as having process-contention scope (user-level) versus system-contention scope (kernel-level).

Mac OS 9 uses cooperative scheduling for threads, where one process controls multiple cooperative threads, and also provides preemptive scheduling for multiprocessing tasks. The kernel schedules multiprocessing tasks using a preemptive scheduling algorithm. All Process Manager processes run within a special multiprocessing task, called the blue task. Gang scheduling runs a set of related threads or processes (a "gang") on a group of processors at the same time, and schedules and de-schedules them together. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. Choose SJF for batch systems where run times are known or can be estimated well; choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the formula for the exponential average used to predict the next CPU burst? [General])
τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n), where t(n) is the length of the most recent actual CPU burst, τ(n) is the previous prediction, and α is a weight between 0 and 1, commonly 1/2. With α = 0 the prediction never changes; with α = 1 only the last burst counts.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § How is the length of the next CPU burst predicted in SJF? [SJF])
Since the scheduler cannot know the future, it predicts the next burst as an exponential average of the past ones: τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n). Here t(n) is the actual length of the most recent burst, τ(n) is the previous prediction, and α is between 0 and 1, commonly 1/2. With α = 0 the prediction never changes; with α = 1 only the last burst matters. With α = 1/2, recent and past history count equally.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Does SJF need to know the burst time in advance? [SJF])

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue: the scheduler takes the process at the head, runs it for at most one quantum, and if it has not finished it is preempted and placed at the tail of the queue.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P1 = 24, P2 = 3, P3 = 3, all arriving at time 0, quantum 4. P1 runs 0–4 and goes to the back. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is Round Robin scheduling? [Round Robin])
Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. [2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. P2 runs 4–7 and finishes, P3 runs 7–10 and finishes, then P1 runs alone from 10 to 30 in five more quanta. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF, but it causes more context switches and long jobs can starve.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the disadvantages of SJF? [SJF])
SJF needs to know the next CPU burst length in advance, which is impossible in general, so it must be predicted. It can starve long processes if short ones keep arriving. The non-preemptive version still lets a long job block a newly arrived short job once the long job has started. It is therefore hard to use as a pure short-term scheduler and is more often used as a model for comparison.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages and disadvantages of SRTF? [SJF])
Advantages: it gives the lowest possible average waiting time among the standard algorithms, and short jobs get a very fast response. Disadvantages: it needs the burst lengths in advance, it causes more context switches than SJF, and long processes can starve. A process that has been preempted must be resumed later, so the scheduler also has to keep track of remaining times.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages and disadvantages of Priority scheduling? [Priority])
Advantages: important processes are served first, and the priority can be tuned to the needs of the system. SJF is itself a special case. Disadvantages: low-priority processes can starve, which is solved by aging; and a preemptive version adds context-switch overhead. Choosing good priorities is also not easy.

Gang scheduling runs a set of related threads or processes (a "gang") on a group of processors at the same time, and schedules and de-schedules them together. Gang scheduling runs a set of related threads or processes (a "gang") on a group of processors at the same time, and schedules and de-schedules them together. It suits parallel programs whose threads communicate and wait on each other, because those threads make no progress while some are running and others are waiting to be scheduled; running them simultaneously avoids that wasted waiting. Round Robin (RR) serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. It is preemptive: a timer interrupt takes the CPU when the quantum expires. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. The time quantum, or time slice, is the maximum continuous CPU time a process may use before it is preempted and sent to the back of the ready queue. It is typically 10 to 100 milliseconds in real systems. In numericals it is given in time units, for example q = 4.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What happens in Round Robin if the time quantum is very large? [Round Robin])

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready process. When a new process arrives with a strictly higher priority than the running one, the running process is preempted and goes back to the ready queue with its remaining time, and the new process runs. An arrival with equal priority does not preempt. Completion times are read off the pieces of the Gantt chart.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. preemptive Priority always runs the arrived process with the highest priority (the lowest priority number). non-preemptive Priority is non-preemptive, whereas preemptive Priority is preemptive. On starvation, non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes, while preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under non-preemptive Priority is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, while under preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption, and preemptive Priority has higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch. Maximise CPU utilisation and throughput. Minimise turnaround time, waiting time and response time. In exams, the comparison between algorithms is usually made on average waiting time and average turnaround time. Some systems also care about fairness and about predictability of response time.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What are the CPU scheduling criteria? [General])
Scheduling algorithms are compared on five criteria. CPU utilisation, keeping the CPU as busy as possible, and throughput, the number of processes completed per unit time, should be maximised. Turnaround time, the time from arrival to completion; waiting time, the time spent in the ready queue; and response time, the time until the first response, should be minimised. In exam numericals the usual comparison is the average waiting time and average turnaround time.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is throughput? [General])
Throughput is the number of processes completed per unit of time. For example, 5 processes finishing in 20 time units give a throughput of 0.25 processes per time unit. Short jobs raise throughput; a long job lowers it. Throughput is one of the criteria to maximise.

[2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Is SJF preemptive or non-preemptive? [SJF])
The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. [1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says Round Robin causes starvation. Is this correct? [Round Robin])
No, that is a common mix-up. Round Robin does not cause starvation: the ready queue is circular, so every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units, where n is the number of processes and q is the quantum. What Round Robin does cause is extra context-switch overhead and a higher average turnaround time than SJF. Starvation is a problem of SJF, SRTF and priority scheduling, where a process can be passed over again and again.

[2] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise Round Robin in a few lines. [Round Robin])
Round Robin (RR) serves a circular FIFO ready queue and gives each process at most one time quantum before moving it to the tail. It is preemptive: a timer interrupt takes the CPU when the quantum expires. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units. Its average waiting time is usually higher than SJF, but bounded for each turn, and its context-switch overhead is the highest, because it switches at every quantum expiry.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does Round Robin cause starvation? [Round Robin])
No. Every process in the ready queue gets the CPU within (n − 1) × q time units, so no process waits forever. Round Robin is starvation-free; its drawback is overhead from context switches, not starvation.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do you draw a Gantt chart? [General])
A Gantt chart is a bar showing which process holds the CPU during each interval of time. To draw one, start at time 0 or at the first arrival; at every scheduling point choose the next process using the algorithm's rule; draw its box for the time it runs; write the start and end times under the box edges. If no process is ready, draw an idle box until the next arrival. The completion time of each process is the end of its last box.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § A student says the idle time at the start of a Gantt chart counts as waiting time. Is that right? [General])
No. Waiting time only counts time a process spends in the ready queue after it has arrived. If the CPU is idle because no process has arrived yet, that idle gap belongs to no process. You still draw the idle gap on the Gantt chart, but each process's waiting time is turnaround − burst, where turnaround starts at that process's own arrival time.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SJF in a few lines. [SJF])

Its average waiting time is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is low, because there is no preemption.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise SRTF in a few lines. [SJF])

Its average waiting time is the lowest of all the standard algorithms, and its context-switch overhead is higher than SJF, because every preemption is a context switch.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is a context switch? [Context switch])
A context switch is the act of saving the state of the currently running process and loading the saved state of the next process to run. The state, including the program counter, registers and memory-management information, is stored in the process control block (PCB). Context switches happen whenever the scheduler moves the CPU from one process to another, for example when a Round Robin quantum expires. They are pure overhead: no user work is done during the switch, so systems try to keep them infrequent.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive Priority scheduling? [Priority])
In non-preemptive Priority scheduling, a newly arrived higher-priority process waits until the running process finishes its burst. In preemptive Priority scheduling it takes the CPU immediately and the running process is put back in the ready queue. Preemptive gives faster service to important work but causes more context switches; both can starve low-priority processes.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling? [SJF])
In non-preemptive (cooperative) scheduling, once a process gets the CPU it keeps it until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. In preemptive scheduling the operating system can take the CPU away from a running process, for example when a timer interrupt fires or when a more important process arrives. FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive. Round Robin and SRTF are preemptive, and priority scheduling can be either. Preemption improves response time but adds context-switch overhead.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Compare preemptive and non-preemptive priority scheduling [Priority])
Both always run the highest-priority ready process. The difference is what happens when a higher-priority process arrives while another is running. In the non-preemptive version, the newcomer is placed at the head of the ready queue and waits until the current burst finishes. In the preemptive version, the running process is interrupted immediately and the newcomer takes the CPU. The preemptive version responds faster to important work but causes more context switches; both can starve low-priority processes without aging.

The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready process. When a new process arrives with a strictly higher priority than the running one, the running process is preempted and goes back to the ready queue with its remaining time, and the new process runs. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive Priority scheduling work step by step? [Priority])
At each scheduling point, collect the processes that have arrived and are not finished, choose the one with the highest priority (smallest number), break ties by arrival time and then process number, and run it to completion. A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
non-preemptive Priority and preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. preemptive Priority always runs the arrived process with the highest priority (the lowest priority number). non-preemptive Priority is non-preemptive, whereas preemptive Priority is preemptive. On starvation, non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes, while preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under non-preemptive Priority is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned, while under preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption, and preemptive Priority has higher than non-preemptive Priority, because every preemption is a context switch. Choose non-preemptive Priority for systems where processes differ in importance and switching must stay cheap; choose preemptive Priority for systems with urgent processes that must run immediately, such as interactive or real-time work.

The basic SJF algorithm is non-preemptive: once a process starts it runs to the end of its burst. The preemptive version is called Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF), where a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the remaining time of the running process takes the CPU.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is non-preemptive scheduling? [Comparison])
In non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks for I/O; the scheduler only runs when the CPU becomes free. FCFS, non-preemptive SJF and non-preemptive Priority scheduling are non-preemptive. It has low overhead and is simple, but a long process can make everyone else wait.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Compare SJF and non-preemptive Priority in detail [Priority])
SJF and non-preemptive Priority differ in how they choose the next process and in what they cost. SJF picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time and runs it to completion. non-preemptive Priority picks, among the processes that have arrived, the one with the highest priority (the lowest priority number) and runs it to completion. Both are non-preemptive. On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Average waiting time under SJF is the minimum among non-preemptive algorithms, while under non-preemptive Priority it is not minimised; it depends on how the priorities are assigned. For context-switch overhead, SJF has low, because there is no preemption, and non-preemptive Priority has low, because there is no preemption. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is a multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ)? [MLFQ])
A multilevel feedback queue is like a multilevel queue except that processes can move between queues based on their behaviour. A new process enters the top queue. A process that uses its full time allotment at a level moves down, so CPU-bound jobs sink to lower-priority queues. Interactive jobs that give up the CPU early stay high. Periodically all jobs may be boosted to the top queue to prevent starvation.

[2] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is a multilevel feedback queue? [Priority])
A multilevel feedback queue has several ready queues with different priorities, and it lets processes move between them. A process that uses its whole quantum, behaving like a CPU-bound job, is moved down to a lower-priority queue. A process that waits too long in a lower queue is moved up, which is a form of aging. Interactive, I/O-bound processes therefore stay in the high-priority queues and get good response time, and no process starves.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the rules of MLFQ? [Priority])
The standard rules are: if the priority of A is higher than B, A runs; if the priorities are equal, they run in Round Robin using the quantum of their queue; a new job enters the highest-priority queue; once a job uses up its time allotment at a level it moves down one queue; and after some period S all jobs are moved to the topmost queue (the priority boost), which prevents starvation and handles jobs whose behaviour changes.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is a multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ)? [MLFQ])
A multilevel feedback queue is like a multilevel queue except that processes can move between queues based on their behaviour. A new process enters the top queue. A process that uses its full time allotment at a level moves down, so CPU-bound jobs sink to lower-priority queues. Interactive jobs that give up the CPU early stay high. Periodically all jobs may be boosted to the top queue to prevent starvation.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Which scheduling algorithms can cause starvation? [SJF])
SJF, SRTF and Priority scheduling can cause starvation: SJF and SRTF starve long jobs, and Priority scheduling starves low-priority processes. FCFS and Round Robin cannot, since every process eventually reaches the head of the queue. Aging fixes starvation in the first group.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does Priority scheduling cause starvation? [Priority])
Yes. A low-priority process can wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving. This is indefinite blocking or starvation. The remedy is aging: gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait for a long time so that they eventually reach the highest priority.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Does SJF cause starvation? [Priority])
Yes. If shorter jobs keep arriving, a long job may be passed over again and again and never get the CPU. That is starvation, also called indefinite blocking. Aging, which gradually raises the priority of a waiting process, is the standard remedy.

[1] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Define waiting time, turnaround time and response time [General])
Turnaround time is the total time from when a process arrives to when it completes: turnaround = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time is the total time the process spends sitting in the ready queue: waiting = turnaround time − burst time. Response time is the time from arrival until the process gets the CPU for the first time: response = first start time − arrival time. For non-preemptive algorithms response time equals waiting time, because once a process starts it runs to completion.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How do you calculate waiting time, turnaround time and response time from a Gantt chart? [General])
Read the completion time of each process off the end of its last box on the chart. Turnaround time = completion time − arrival time. Waiting time = turnaround time − burst time. Response time = the start of the process's first box − its arrival time. Then average each column over all processes. An alternative for waiting time is to add up every interval the process spent ready but not running.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is the difference between turnaround time and waiting time? [General])
Turnaround time is the total time from arrival to completion, so it includes waiting in the ready queue and actually running on the CPU. Waiting time counts only the time spent in the ready queue. Therefore turnaround time = waiting time + burst time, and turnaround time is always at least as large as waiting time.

A higher-priority process that arrives while another is running must wait until the running one finishes. Then repeat.

Shortest job next. Shortest job next (SJN), also known as shortest job first (SJF) or shortest process next (SPN), is a scheduling policy that selects for execution the waiting process with the smallest execution time. SJN is a non-preemptive algorithm. Shortest remaining time is a preemptive variant of SJN. Shortest job next is advantageous because of its simplicity and because it minimizes the average amount of time each process has to wait until its execution is complete. However, it has the potential for process starvation for processes which will require a long time to complete if short processes are continually added. Highest response ratio next is similar but provides a solution to this problem using a technique called aging. Another disadvantage of using shortest job next is that the total execution time of a job must be known before execution. While it is impossible to predict execution time perfectly, several methods can be used to estimate it, such as a weighted average of previous execution times. Multilevel feedback queue can also be used to approximate SJN without the need for the total execution time oracle. Shortest job next can be effectively used with interactive processes which generally follow a pattern of alternating between waiting for a command and executing it. If the execution burst of a process is regarded as a separate "job", the past behaviour can indicate which process to run next, based on an estimate of its running time. Shortest job next is used in specialized environments where accurate estimates of running time are available.

On starvation, SJF can starve long jobs if shorter jobs keep arriving, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. [1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does non-preemptive SJF work step by step? [SJF])
Start at time 0 or at the first arrival. At each scheduling point, collect all the processes that have arrived and not finished. Pick the one with the smallest burst time; break ties by earlier arrival. Run it to completion, move the clock forward by its burst time, and repeat. If no process is ready, jump the clock to the next arrival and draw an idle gap.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is SRTF scheduling? [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, its burst is compared with the remaining time of the running process; if the new burst is strictly shorter, the running process is preempted and the new one runs. The preempted process returns to the ready queue with its remaining time. SRTF gives an even lower average waiting time than non-preemptive SJF.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § Explain Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling [SJF])
Shortest Remaining Time First is the preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the newcomer needs less time, the running process is preempted and the newcomer runs. For example, if P1 has 7 units left and P2 arrives needing only 4, P2 takes the CPU. [2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages and disadvantages of SRTF? [SJF])
Advantages: it gives the lowest possible average waiting time among the standard algorithms, and short jobs get a very fast response. Disadvantages: it needs the burst lengths in advance, it causes more context switches than SJF, and long processes can starve. A process that has been preempted must be resumed later, so the scheduler also has to keep track of remaining times.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the advantages and disadvantages of Priority scheduling? [Priority])
Advantages: important processes are served first, and the priority can be tuned to the needs of the system. SJF is itself a special case. Disadvantages: low-priority processes can starve, which is solved by aging; and a preemptive version adds context-switch overhead. Choosing good priorities is also not easy.

Context from the course material:
[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the rules of MLFQ? [Priority])
The standard rules are: if the priority of A is higher than B, A runs; if the priorities are equal, they run in Round Robin using the quantum of their queue; a new job enters the highest-priority queue; once a job uses up its time allotment at a level it moves down one queue; and after some period S all jobs are moved to the topmost queue (the priority boost), which prevents starvation and handles jobs whose behaviour changes.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is a multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ)? [MLFQ])
A multilevel feedback queue is like a multilevel queue except that processes can move between queues based on their behaviour. A new process enters the top queue. A process that uses its full time allotment at a level moves down, so CPU-bound jobs sink to lower-priority queues. Interactive jobs that give up the CPU early stay high. Periodically all jobs may be boosted to the top queue to prevent starvation.

[3] (notes/analogies_and_doubts.md § What is a multilevel feedback queue? [Priority])
A multilevel feedback queue has several ready queues with different priorities, and it lets processes move between them. A process that uses its whole quantum, behaving like a CPU-bound job, is moved down to a lower-priority queue. A process that waits too long in a lower queue is moved up, which is a form of aging. Interactive, I/O-bound processes therefore stay in the high-priority queues and get good response time, and no process starves.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is a multilevel queue scheduler? [Comparison])
A multilevel queue scheduler splits the ready queue into several separate queues, such as foreground (interactive) and background (batch) processes. Each queue has its own scheduling algorithm, for example Round Robin for the foreground queue and FCFS for the background queue. There is also scheduling between the queues, either fixed priority or time slicing. A process stays in the queue it was assigned to.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What are the types of schedulers? [Comparison])
There are three types of schedulers: the long-term (job) scheduler, which admits jobs into memory and controls the degree of multiprogramming; the medium-term scheduler, which swaps processes out of and back into memory; and the short-term (CPU) scheduler, which chooses the next ready process to run and runs very often. FCFS, SJF, Priority and Round Robin are short-term (CPU) scheduling algorithms.

[3] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § Why do we need a ready queue and a dispatcher? [General])
The ready queue stores the processes that can run, and the scheduler picks one from it. The dispatcher then actually gives the CPU to the chosen process by switching context, switching to user mode and jumping to the right place in the program. The scheduler decides, the dispatcher acts.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is load balancing on a multiprocessor system? [General])
Load balancing moves processes between the per-CPU ready queues of a multiprocessor system so that no CPU sits idle while another has a backlog. Push migration has a periodic task check the queues and push processes from a busy CPU to an idle one; pull migration has an idle CPU pull a waiting process from a busy one. Load balancing works against processor affinity, since moving a process to balance load also throws away its cache state, so real schedulers trade the two off.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is multiprocessor scheduling? [General])
Multiprocessor scheduling decides how ready processes are spread across more than one CPU. In symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) every processor runs the scheduler and picks from a shared ready queue, which needs locking to avoid two CPUs grabbing the same process. An alternative is asymmetric multiprocessing, where only one designated processor makes scheduling decisions and the rest execute user code, which is simpler but that one processor can become a bottleneck.

Round Robin is a preemptive algorithm designed for time-sharing systems. Each process is given a small unit of CPU time called the time quantum or time slice. [2] (notes/cpu_scheduling_notes.md § Round Robin (RR) [Round Robin])
Round Robin is designed for time-sharing systems. It is similar to FCFS but adds preemption: a small unit of time called a time quantum or time slice, generally 10 to 100 milliseconds, is defined, and the ready queue is treated as a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler picks the first process, sets a timer to interrupt after one quantum and dispatches it. If the process has a burst shorter than the quantum it releases the CPU itself; otherwise the timer goes off, a context switch happens and the process is put at the tail of the ready queue. Round Robin queue order rule. When a process arrives at the same moment that the running process's quantum expires, or during the slice, the newly arrived process is added to the ready queue before the preempted process is put back at the tail. Getting this order wrong is the most common error in RR numericals and changes every waiting time after that point. Round Robin worked example. Waiting times are P1 = 10 − 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, so the average waiting time is 17 / 3 = 5.67.

[1] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § How does FCFS work step by step? [FCFS])
First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.

On starvation, FCFS cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue, while non-preemptive Priority can starve low-priority processes if higher-priority ones keep arriving, which aging fixes. Under Round Robin every process gets its first turn within (n − 1) × q time units, so response time is short and predictable. That is why Round Robin suits interactive systems and FCFS suits batch systems.

First, order the processes by arrival time, and by process number if arrival times are equal. Second, run the first process to completion. Third, when it finishes, take the next process from the head of the queue; if it has not arrived yet, the CPU idles until it does. Fourth, repeat until all are done. Finally compute completion, turnaround = completion − arrival and waiting = turnaround − burst for each process.

[2] (notes/algorithm_reference.md § What is FCFS scheduling? [FCFS])
First Come First Served is the simplest CPU scheduling algorithm. The process that arrives first in the ready queue gets the CPU first and keeps it until it finishes or blocks for I/O. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join at the tail and the CPU is given to the process at the head. FCFS is non-preemptive.

[3] (notes/algorithm_facts_generated.md § Summarise FCFS in a few lines. [FCFS])
First Come First Served (FCFS) runs the ready process that arrived first, strictly in arrival order. It is non-preemptive: a running process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. On starvation, it cannot starve any process, because every process eventually reaches the head of the FIFO queue. Its average waiting time is often long and very sensitive to the order of arrival, and its context-switch overhead is the lowest, because there is no preemption.
